q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

sentences.sentence: Marshall McLuhan proposed the four "laws of media" in the mid-1970s, describing them as "a rigorous means of investigating" the effects of artefacts on people and society [3].
The four were collected in book form in *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988), written with his son Eric McLuhan [3].

The laws take the form of four questions asked of any artefact: what does it enhance or intensify; what does it obsolesce or displace; what does it retrieve that was previously obsolesced; and what does it become when pressed to an extreme [20].

Tyler's summary of the radio case shows how the quadrants were meant to interlock: radio amplifies the voice to "simultaneous access to the entire planet", obsolesces print as the vehicle of breaking news, retrieves the town crier, and reverses into television [3].
All four aspects are inherent in each artifact from the start" [20].

Library and Archives Canada's curatorial account stresses the same point, noting that although "McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order" [1].
Tyler likewise cites *Laws of Media* page 99 for the simultaneity of the four laws [3].
The McLuhans say the four were found by asking "What general, verifiable (that is, testable) statements can be made about all media?" and that they "were surprised to find only four" [20].
Schumann, summarising the book, reports that McLuhan held the four laws "valid for all the artifacts of man and challenged all to find counter examples" [20].

In the book the McLuhans disclaim an underlying theory: "We propose no underlying theory to attack or defend, but rather a heuristic device, a set of four questions, which we call a tetrad", adding that the four questions can be asked, and the answers checked, by anyone anywhere at any time about any human artefact [20].
Tyler treats the checkability sentence as Eric McLuhan's own reproducibility claim, quoting it from *Laws of Media* page 7 [3].
On a single page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206) they give two different tetrads for wine [3].
The second has it enhancing food and "the occasion", obsolescing "inhibition", retrieving "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reversing into "hangover" and insult [3].

Tyler's inference is that "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [3].
McLuhan calls it "an instrument for revealing and predicting the dynamics of situations and innovations" [20].
It also sits awkwardly with McLuhan's reported rule against forecasting, which Tyler quotes as "Never predict anything that hasn't already happened" [3].

Library and Archives Canada's exhibition, which attributes its wording to *Laws of Media* page 116 and to Robert Babe's book, says the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool", but a device for exploring the grammar and syntax of an artefact and describing "situations that are in process" [1].
The same page describes the laws as pedagogical instruments, "meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [1].
As the archive's account notes, citing Babe, the fourth law — that an artefact reverses into an opposing form when it is overheated — "marks a significant departure from Innis" [1].

The McLuhan circle's later defence adopts the heuristic reading outright: in a *Canadian Journal of Communication* article co-authored by Eric McLuhan, a probe "is not a thing but a happening, an event", whose "virtue (i.e., power)" lies "in its launching and relaunchability" [15].
As a probe, this "tetrad" can "provide illuminating insights" into the effects of individual technologies [3].

First, it is too loose: "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into", so "The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit" [3].
Second, it is too rigid: "just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps" [3].
On a single page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206) they give two different tetrads for wine [3].
The first has wine enhancing "grape juice" through fermentation, obsolescing "commonplace flavours", retrieving "ritual observance", and reversing into "cooking wine vinegar" [3].
The second, on the same page, has it enhancing food and "the occasion", obsolescing "inhibition", retrieving "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reversing into "hangover" and insult [3].

Tyler's inference is that "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [3].
"And yet the tetrad has its uses" [3].

His salvage is the probe reading, quoting McLuhan's "I don't explain - I explore" and insisting the tetrad forces attention onto the artefact's "operation and effects" rather than the content of particular broadcasts or bottles [3].

He then sets the price of that salvage: "The diversity of results from the tetrad's application need not be a problem--once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity--so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [3].

The Kaiser Family Foundation's panel of 8- to 18-year-olds found that heavy users of one medium are heavy users of others, so the looked-for "displacement effect" did not appear; Nick Yee's survey of massively multiplayer online players found the opposite, with 21.0 hours a week of play alongside 7.7 hours of television against a national average near 28 [3].
Tyler's conclusion is that "existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [3].

He then rescues the quadrant by redefining it: obsolescence is not extinction, since newspapers did not die out with radio, "any more than "commonplace flavours" disappeared with the consumption of wine" [3].

Logan, McLuhan's collaborator at Toronto, writes that "LOMs are not strictly scientific laws", because "a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into", and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [2].

The anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, applying the tetrad to the Internet, calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" but treats them as a usable first cut that "needs supplementing" before it yields "a more accurate reflection" [13].

The political-economy objection, as Library and Archives Canada's exhibition summarises it, is that without a political dimension the analysis "quickly collapses into a strictly cultural one, bereft of an account of how capital and power operate within a globalized structure" [7].

The decolonial objection is that "his valorization of oral culture is often Orientalist and romantic", and that McLuhan's global village "failed to account for the power dynamics in a globalized media environment" [7].

The wider field-level version of that charge, from Last Moyo, is that media and communication studies "lie at the centre of Euro-American modernity" and that decolonisation "must decentre Eurocentrism and imperial theories" [6].

Graham Harman argues the tetrad applies to all objects and not only human artefacts, since every object is a medium; media-ecology scholars took that up explicitly, treating human-made, animal-made and natural screens as media in an article that "takes this framework in considering the screen as medium" [14].

A 2016 article in *Glocality* runs the four questions on the smartphone and concludes that the tetrad "is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments" [8].

Its reversal quadrant looks forward to augmented reality and Google Glass, and it concedes that multiple readings are unavoidable, since an interpretation of the tetrad "is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [8].

The same author closes by declining to settle anything: "one cannot say with certainty what McLuhan would say about the smartphone", and the tetrad offers "an understanding and interpretation" rather than a finding [8].
An Indonesian communication journal applied the four laws to telemedicine during Covid-19 by reviewing 23 international journals published between 2015 and 2020 [9].

Its reversal quadrant is the most substantive part of the exercise: telemedicine "appears to provide equal opportunities for everyone to get health services but when pushed to the limit of its potential, telemedicine can only have an optimal impact on good communicator, digital divide, and financial capability" [9].

Michael Bolton, a software-testing consultant, recast the four laws as four "testing heuristics" in *Better Software* in October 2007, asking what a feature or an organisational change enhances, obsolesces, retrieves and reverses into [12].

The first is Iseri and Logan's, which "extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU)" alongside the original Laws of Media, so that environments and users each get their own four quadrants rather than appearing only as the object of a medium's effects [2].

The second is the Harman-inspired extension to non-human-made artefacts, which produced tetrads of human-made, animal-made and natural screens, treating the tetrad as a way of knowing rather than a predictive law and arguing that the wider application strengthens it [14].

The third is comparative: a 2013 article in *Explorations in Media Ecology* merges the tetrad with Claude Lévi-Strauss's canonical formula for myth, on the ground that both are four-part figure-ground structures [10].
McLuhan, he writes, prescribed the four effects as a complement to Aristotle's four causes, and "The invitation is to try them out on your own terms and topics" [10].

Digital media, he writes, "enhance interactivity, access to information, and two-way communication", "obsolesce mass media, such as television and newspapers", "retrieve community", and "pushed far enough, they flip or reverse into hyperreality or the loss of contact with nature and our bodies" [22].

He then proposes a reversal the McLuhans did not: with digital media the direction of extension inverts, and the user becomes an extension of the medium, because "every key stroke and choice they make is information that is fed into that Big Data system" [22].
He draws on Rushkoff's account of captology and on McLuhan's own 1969 line that "The more the data banks record about each one of us, the less we exist" [22].

Two reference works anchor the applied tradition. *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan* (2017) collects unpublished tetrads with an index, including a chapter on tetrad development and submissions that documents how the McLuhans solicited tetrads from others [19].
Library and Archives Canada's exhibition carries the same teaching material, including the standard exercise "Can you apply the laws of media to the cellular telephone?" [19].

Tyler's own application is the partial exception, because he uses quadrants to attack named misconceptions: Berger's claim that solo gaming is alienating, the assumption that games displace television, the "immersive fallacy" of inevitable total immersion, and the idea of the magic circle as a sealed realm [3].
Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting investigation is ultimately constructive" [3].
If a medium obsolesces something, the effect should be visible as displacement, and Tyler assembles the studies that would show it [3].
The Kaiser Family Foundation's surveys of 8- to 18-year-olds found that heavy users of one medium tend to be heavy users of others, so the expected "displacement effect" did not appear [3].

Nick Yee's survey of massively multiplayer players found the opposite, reporting 21.0 hours a week of play against 7.7 hours of television, a total close to the national average for television alone, which Yee read as support for displacement [3].
Tyler's conclusion is that "existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [3].

The McLuhans did not claim one medium replaces another, and Tyler redefines obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction, noting McLuhan's point that more handwriting is done daily now than before printing [3].
The McLuhans' two wine tetrads on one page suggest they would not [3].

Reversal makes this harder, because McLuhan's rule was never to predict anything that has not already happened [3], and Hempell's account of the method has the analyst working from "historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject" with no coding rules or comparison case [21].

The WebAIM Million audits one million home pages each year with a fixed automated engine, detecting 56,114,377 distinct accessibility errors in its February 2026 sample, an average of 56.1 per page, and reports that "95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures", up from 94.8% in 2025 [16].
It also states the limit of its own instrument: "Absence of detected errors does not indicate that a page is accessible or conformant" [16].

Disability scholarship locates the effect in "a built environment and organized social activity that preclude or restrict the participation of people seen or labeled as having disabilities", which makes the unit of analysis interactional rather than social [5].
The WHO's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health formalises disability as a dynamic interaction between a health condition and environmental and personal factors [5].

Empirical work in that frame finds media effects distributed unevenly: Pacheco and Burgess, surveying 960 New Zealand adult internet users, found that "people with disabilities have restricted fibre access and higher wireless broadband (a much slower connection type)" and "use social media platforms less" [18].
Statistics Canada publishes comparable Canadian data on the barriers to internet access experienced by persons with disabilities [17].

Hempell's media-ecology account describes the tetrad as deliberately non-causal: McLuhan "proposed the tetrad as an alternate means for discussing the effect of technology on society", organising an artefact as a "resonating interval" instead of using "a model based on causality" [21].
McLuhan and Powers go further, describing a tetrad that "performs the function of myth in that it compresses past, present, and future into one through the power of simultaneity" [21].

Logan states the reason it cannot be more: a tetrad makes no unique prediction about what will be retrieved or what a medium will flip into, and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions" [2].
Eriksen states the condition of use: the laws are overambitious and deterministic, and the model can be "a starting-point (although it needs supplementing)" [13].

Tyler states the test of quality: diversity of answers is acceptable only "once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity" and only where the results provide "illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [3].
Are the two dualisms that generate the four boxes stated, in Harman's sense, so that the fourfold is not merely decoration [14]?
A reliability study would measure whether independent analysts, given a written protocol, converge on the same four answers; the two wine tetrads predict they would not [3].
A prediction ledger would date and score each forward claim; the fourth law's exclusion of forecasts [3] means only claims about potential already realised could be scored.
A disaggregated version would answer the second law per population rather than for society, which existing disability and access statistics could support [18].
No published study located for this report tested the tetrad, and its own practitioners describe the method as unstructured expert judgment [21].
The framework probably cannot be tested in its own terms, because the tradition presents it as non-causal and myth-like [21].
The claim that the tetrad is "not meant to be a scientific tool" [1] is now the mainstream reading, including in the institutions that curate McLuhan's papers.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: Official Canadian government account: the four laws are simultaneous, non-chronological, and the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool" but an exploratory instrument for the "grammar and syntax" of artefacts — the media-ecology reading of its status.

notes.quote: These four laws of media further exhibit McLuhan's abiding concern with pedagogy: they are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce. McLuhan phrased them as questions with which to consider any artefact:
notes.claim: Library and Archives Canada's official McLuhan exhibition page presents the four laws as pedagogical tools for analysing the patterns of effects of any technology.

notes.quote: As Robert Babe has noted, the fourth law -- that an artefact reverses into an opposing form when "overheated" -- marks a significant departure from Innis.
notes.claim: McLuhan's fourth law — reversal into an opposing form when "overheated" — is a departure from Innis, per Robert Babe, cited in the government exhibition.

notes.quote: There is one caveat about the term laws in McLuhan’s Laws of Media, and that is that LOMs are not strictly scientific laws. This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into. The LOM is more of an exploratory tool or probe that provides insights into the effects of a new medium or technology and its possible evolution, and there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM.
notes.claim: Toronto media-ecology scholar Robert K. Logan (with Iseri) insists the tetrad is not a strictly scientific law but an exploratory probe with multiple valid answers — the fidelity position of the Toronto School.

notes.quote: Marshall McLuhan’s Laws of Media (LOM), which describe the evolution of artifacts in terms of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal (or flip) are extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU).
notes.claim: A named extension of the tetrad: Iseri and Logan (2016) add parallel tetrads for media environments and media users, tripling the four laws into LOM/LOME/LOMU.

notes.quote: McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175). His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in _Laws of Media_, co-written with his father, that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7).
notes.claim: The McLuhans themselves claimed the tetrad was a falsifiable scientific method, checked by anyone anywhere — the claim any empirical test would have to hold them to.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal "scientific method", the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit. At the same time, just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps.
notes.claim: The double bind that blocks testing: too vague to falsify, yet rigid enough to force an answer in every quadrant; so a test must specify procedures that constrain the analyst.

notes.quote: This particular McLuhanesque method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles: that is, bothersome empiric elements which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn in order that they be made to fit.
notes.claim: Tom Tyler (Oxford Brookes), in a DiGRA 2007 conference paper built entirely around the tetrad, opens by naming the central criticism: the tetrad is Procrustean, forcing awkward empirical detail to fit its four boxes. This is the canonical statement of the "Procrustean rigidity" charge, from a sympathetic user rather than a hostile critic.

notes.claim: Tyler's double bind: read as science the tetrad is simultaneously unfalsifiable (anything can be stretched to fit) and rigid (all four quadrants must be filled). His proof is that the McLuhans give two different tetrads for wine on the same page of Laws of Media (p. 206), so "it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by 'anyone, anywhere, at any time'" — undermining Eric McLuhan's own reproducibility claim.

notes.quote: The idea that these are “scientific laws” in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous. And yet the tetrad has its uses.
notes.claim: The verdict of a sympathetic critic: the claim to scientific law is "preposterous", but the tetrad survives as a "probe"/set of questions; "The diversity of responses to its application need not be a problem—once we lose the cod-scientific rhetoric—so long as these provide illuminating insights." This is the retreat-to-analogy/heuristic position in its most explicit form.

notes.claim: Applied tetrad on a digital device (smartphone), peer-reviewed in Glocality (Ubiquity Press): the author treats the tetrad as universally applicable and uses its reversal quadrant to speculate about AR/Google Glass — an application, not a test.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: The same applied tetrad concedes that answers are reader-dependent — "multiple interpretations are possible" — which is the probe framing Toronto-school scholars insist on, appearing inside an applied digital-media tetrad.

notes.quote: McLuhan prescribed his so-called Four Effects (laws of media) as a complementary method to Aristotle’s well-known Four Causes: Material, Efficient, Formal, and Final.
notes.claim: Sandstrom (Social Epistemology Review and Reply Collective) presents the tetrad as an extension of Aristotle's four causes and as an open method inviting others to apply it to their own topics — the "extend it by using it" programme.

notes.quote: The invitation is to try them out on your own terms and topics and see what effects you can discover in the emergence of new (or old) media.
notes.claim: Sandstrom's framing of how the tetrad is meant to travel: an invitation to apply it to any topic, which is how applied tetrads spread in the literature.

notes.quote: Perhaps the best-known example is the WHO’s International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (World Health Organization 2001, referred to as ICF), which emphasizes that disability is a “dynamic interaction between health conditions and environmental and personal factors”.
notes.claim: The WHO's ICF — the official framework disability policy uses — defines disability as a measurable interaction between health condition and environmental/personal factors. This is what an empirically testable version of "what does this medium obsolesce, for whom" would look like, and it is the standard against which the tetrad's undifferentiated answers fall short.

notes.quote: This has led to the phenomenon of a technological fix or ‘techno-solutionism’, the dealing with a problem through a the implementation of an artifact or artifactual process, where it is questionable, to say the least, whether this is the best way, or even an acceptable way, of dealing with the problem.
notes.claim: Philosophy of technology names the failure mode the accessibility critique attributes to tetrad readings: asserting that an artefact resolves a problem without evidence about who bears the costs — "techno-solutionism".

notes.quote: McLuhan proposed that every medium can be submitted to fourprobes—testing heuristics— that he called the Laws of Media
notes.claim: A practitioner account (software-testing consultant Michael Bolton, in Better Software, citing Federman and de Kerckhove's McLuhan for Managers) treats the four laws as heuristic probes for anticipating effects of new products — the design/strategy-agency reading of the tetrad as an ideation and foresight tool rather than a truth claim.

notes.quote: The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: Library and Archives Canada's curatorial account of the tetrad explicitly denies it is a scientific instrument, reading it as an exploratory, pedagogical tool for the "grammar and syntax" of artefacts — the Toronto School/media-ecology position that the testability claim should be dropped rather than tested.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order.
notes.claim: Any test design must respect the McLuhans' claim that the four laws operate simultaneously rather than in sequence — which rules out treating them as stages or as sequential predictions, and explains why "reversal" is so hard to score.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: An anthropologist applying the tetrad to the Internet concedes the laws are "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" but treats them as a usable first cut that must be supplemented and broken down by level (technological, social, cultural) — the applied-scholar compromise position.

notes.quote: McLuhan's model can be a starting-point (although it needs supplementing) for a more accurate reflection on these issues.
notes.claim: Eriksen states the minimum condition for using the tetrad seriously: it needs supplementing before it yields "a more accurate reflection" — i.e. the framework alone is insufficient, additional distinctions must be added by the analyst.

notes.quote: McLuhan proposed that every medium can be submitted to fourprobes—testing heuristics— that he called the Laws of Media (see the StickyNotes for a reference).
notes.claim: Applied tetrad in a software-testing trade magazine (Better Software, Oct 2007, Michael Bolton, Toronto): the four laws recast as four "testing heuristics" for evaluating requirements, features and organisational changes such as a dedicated test team — the tetrad travelling into professional practice as a probe rather than a predictive law.

notes.quote: Following Graham Harman in the charge that Marshall and Eric McLuhan’s laws of media are applicable beyond human-made artefacts, this article takes this framework in considering the screen as medium.
notes.claim: A named extension from media-ecology scholars at Drexel University (Grodsky, Hildebrand, Hakanen, Explorations in Media Ecology 17:1, 2018): following Graham Harman's charge that the laws apply beyond human-made artefacts, they formulate tetrads of human-made, animal-made and natural screens, treating the tetrad as an epistemology rather than a predictive law — and argue this wider application "strengthens" it.

notes.quote: A probe is not a thing but a happening, an event. It is the equivalent of a verb in the infinitive form. In the same way the life of an arrow does not lie in sitting there but in being shot into the air, the virtue (i.e., power) of a probe lies in its launching and relaunchability.
notes.claim: In a peer-reviewed article co-authored by Eric McLuhan (Canadian Journal of Communication, 2013), the McLuhan circle itself defines the status of the laws as "probes" — events to be relaunched rather than true/false propositions, which is why the authors perform rather than defend McLuhanism.

notes.quote: Across the one million home pages, 56,114,377 distinct accessibility errors were detected—an average of 56.1 errors per page.
notes.claim: The contrast case for section 4: accessibility research routinely runs population-scale, standardised, repeatable measurement of what a medium (the web) actually does to its users — one million home pages scored by a fixed engine. Tetrad scholarship has produced nothing comparable: its "laws" are illustrated by example, never scored at scale. (WebAIM Million, 2026 report, February 2026 sample.)

notes.quote: 95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures. This number increased from 94.8% in 2025—reversing a trend of small improvements each of the previous 6 years.
notes.claim: A quantified prevalence estimate, with a stated denominator and year-on-year trend, of the kind an empirically testable claim about a medium's effects takes: 95.9% of the top million home pages fail the WCAG 2 standard (Feb 2026), up from 94.8% in 2025.

notes.quote: Differences in the number and proportions of persons with disabilities or long-term conditions aged 15 years and over in Canada who experienced at least one type of barrier to accessibility when accessing the Internet because of their condition.
notes.claim: Official statistical infrastructure already collects the disaggregated "who is affected" data that a tetrad never specifies: Statistics Canada Table 13-10-0938 measures the share of persons with disabilities who hit at least one Internet access barrier (published 2025-03-24, reference year 2024). An empirical test of "what this medium enhances/obsolesces, and for whom" could be built on such data; tetrad literature does not use it.

notes.quote: Results show people with disabilities have restricted fibre access and higher wireless broadband (a much slower connection type). People with disabilities use social media platforms less and are more concerned about certain online risks.
notes.claim: An empirical communication study (Pacheco & Burgess, n=960 New Zealand adult internet users, published in Disability & Society 2024) finds a medium's effects distributed unevenly across publics rather than uniform: disabled users get worse connection types and use social media less. This is the interactional, group-differentiated finding a society-level tetrad answer cannot express — and the kind of study that could supply a real test.

notes.quote: Can you apply the laws of media to the cellular telephone?
notes.claim: Same LAC page also carries the applied cell-phone tetrad, the canonical demonstration case used to teach the method.

notes.quote: Absence of detected errors does not indicate that a page is accessible or conformant.
notes.claim: The measurement discipline the tetrad never adopts: the largest empirical accessibility programme states plainly that non-detection is not confirmation. A falsifiable tetrad would need exactly this kind of stated instrument limitation.

notes.quote: We propose no underlying theory to attack or defend, but rather a heuristic device, a set of four questions, which we call a tetrad. They can be asked (and the answers checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artifact).
notes.claim: The McLuhans' own statement of status, quoted from Laws of Media in a practitioner's account: they explicitly disclaimed proposing a theory, calling the tetrad a "heuristic device" whose answers anyone can check about any artefact — at once a disclaimer of scientific theory and a claim of universal checkability.

notes.quote: McLuhan postulated that the four laws he discovered were valid for all the artifacts of man and challenged all to find counter examples.
notes.claim: Key point on the laws' claimed scope and testability: the McLuhans presented the four laws as universally valid for all artefacts and threw down a falsification challenge — find a counter-example — which is exactly the criterion later critics said the tetrad cannot meet.

notes.quote: The tetrad of the effects of technologies and artifacts presents not a sequential process, but rather four simultaneous ones. All four aspects are inherent in each artifact from the start.
notes.claim: The McLuhans' claim that the four effects are simultaneous and inherent in every artefact from the outset — not stages in a sequence — stated in their own words as quoted from Laws of Media.

notes.quote: McLuhan proposed the tetrad as an alternate means for discussing the effect of technology on society. Instead of using a model based on causality, the tetrad organizes an artifact as a "resonating interval": an object which transcends time; and is affected by both its own attributes and the environment which surrounds it.
notes.claim: The media-ecology reading (Hempell, 1996) states the tetrad is deliberately non-causal, an "alternate means for discussing" effects — so on this reading there is nothing to test, since no causal claim is made; a test would first have to convert the tetrad into a causal hypothesis it was designed not to be.

notes.quote: ...the tetrad performs the function of myth in that it compresses past, present, and future into one through the power of simultaneity.
notes.claim: McLuhan and Powers' own framing, quoted approvingly in the media-ecology literature: the tetrad works like myth, compressing time through simultaneity — an aesthetic/interpretive status incompatible with falsification, and the strongest internal obstacle to empirical testing.

notes.quote: Additionally, the tetrad allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments.
notes.claim: Even sympathetic practitioners scale the claim down from prediction to "speculate": the tetrad's forward-looking quadrant (reversal) is offered as speculation, not a forecast that could be scored against later outcomes.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed applied tetrad (Adam, Glocality, 2016) concedes that results are analyst-dependent — each quadrant answer rests on the interpreter's own perceptions — exactly the condition any test must remedy with specified procedures and independent coders.

notes.quote: The tetrad is arrived at through a process of asking questions, based on historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject:
notes.claim: The method as actually practised is unstructured expert judgment — four questions answered from the analyst's "historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject" — with no coding rules, sampling frame, or comparison case, so a test would have to supply the procedure the tradition leaves open.

notes.quote: Of course, one cannot say with certainty what McLuhan would say about the smartphone and all the other new technologies of the last decades. However, following his key concepts and the tetrad model as a framework offers an understanding and interpretation of the smartphone as a new medium in the context of our cultural and technological evolution.
notes.claim: An applied tetrad explicitly declines to settle anything: its conclusion offers only interpretation and speculation about the medium's future, conceding "one cannot say with certainty." If applications of this kind were the field's empirical tests, they would have to yield checkable predictions; they yield interpretations instead.

notes.quote: Considered as a _scientific_ _theory_, McLuhan's four "laws of media" risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner. Conceived as an _exploratory probe_, however, this "tetrad" can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies.
notes.claim: The peer-reviewed journal version (Game Studies, vol. 8 no. 2, Dec 2008, ISSN 1604-7982) of Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe" states the charge in its sharpest form: as a scientific theory the tetrad "risk[s] violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner", while as a probe it is defensible. Useful to the writer as the citable journal-of-record statement of both the Procrustean charge and the retreat to heuristic/probe — distinct venue from the DiGRA 2007 proceedings version.

notes.quote: McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175). His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in _Laws of Media_, co-written with his father, that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7). This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans' own examples illustrates.
notes.claim: Identifies precisely what the critics are attacking: the McLuhans themselves claimed Popperian falsifiability and universal reproducibility ("anyone, anywhere, at any time", Laws of Media p. 7), so unfalsifiability is a charge about the McLuhans' own self-description, not a critic's invention — and Tyler's evidence is the McLuhans' own inconsistent wine tetrads on p. 206. Note the page's other finding: applied to games, the empirical literature on "displacement" of television is "inconclusive or equivocal" (Beentjes et al.; Kaiser Family Foundation vs Nick Yee), i.e. the second law resists confirmation.

notes.quote: In the mid 1970s, McLuhan proposed what he called the "Laws of Media", a rigorous means of investigating "the operation and effects of human artefacts on man and society" (1977, p. 175)
notes.claim: Tyler dates the laws to the mid-1970s and records McLuhan's own description of them as "a rigorous means of investigating" the effects of artefacts — the scientific framing, before the 1988 book.

notes.quote: The four 'laws', we are told, operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (McLuhan & McLuhan, 1988, p. 99), and thus, considered as a heuristic device, afford a means for interrogating what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium.
notes.claim: Tyler cites Laws of Media p. 99 for simultaneity, and reads the consequence: as a heuristic the tetrad interrogates what is already implicit in a medium rather than forecasting.

notes.quote: The question seems to invite speculation regarding future developments, but McLuhan himself always urged that one should "Never predict anything that hasn't already happened" (quoted in Federman, 2006).
notes.claim: The reversal quadrant is not futurology: McLuhan's own rule was never to predict anything that has not already happened, which limits what the fourth law can be scored against.

notes.quote: McLuhan was not simply claiming that one medium entirely supersedes another: clearly, newspapers did not die out with the advent of radio any more than "commonplace flavours" disappeared with the consumption of wine.
notes.claim: Tyler's working definition of obsolescence: not extinction but displacement of a function, which is why the second law resists a simple displacement test.

notes.quote: Digital new media **enhance** interactivity, access to information, and two-way communication. They **obsolesce** mass media, such as television and newspapers. They **retrieve** community. And pushed far enough, they **flip or reverse** into hyperreality or the loss of contact with nature and our bodies.
notes.claim: Logan's peer-reviewed applied tetrad on digital media: four answers given as flat assertions (enhance interactivity, obsolesce mass media, retrieve community, flip into hyperreality), plus a second reversal he proposes — that users become extensions of their media. Application, not test.

notes.quote: Concrete comparative research into the use and impact of 'new' or 'interactive' media such as digital games has tended to be either inconclusive or equivocal on the question of such a displacement, however.
notes.claim: Empirical studies bearing on the tetrad's second law (obsolescence/displacement of television by games) already exist and are reviewed by Tyler: the Kaiser Family Foundation panel found new media did not displace TV (heavy users of one medium are heavy users of others), while Nick Yee's MMORPG survey found the opposite. So the tetrad's claims have in fact attracted empirical testing, and the results are equivocal — contradicting the section's claim that the literature contains no such study.

notes.quote: "The tetrad - the four laws considered together as a cluster - is an instrument for revealing and predicting the dynamics of situations and innovations," wrote McLuhan.
notes.claim: In Laws of Media itself (quoted by Schumann) the McLuhans describe the tetrad as an instrument for "predicting" — evidence against the section's conclusion that the fourth law is "not a forecast".

notes.quote: The tetrad was found by asking, 'What general, verifiable (that is, testable) statements can be made about all media?'
notes.claim: Immediately after the "no underlying theory" disclaimer, the McLuhans say the tetrad was derived from asking what "verifiable (that is, testable)" statements can be made about all media — so they did present it as offering testable statements, not as declining to offer anything refutable.

notes.quote: 12. McLuhan, _Laws of Media_, p. 116.
notes.claim: The exhibition page's own footnote attributes the "not meant to be a scientific tool" passage to Laws of Media p. 116, i.e. it is McLuhan's own text, not Library and Archives Canada's independent curatorial reading (the page cites published books, not the McLuhan papers).

notes.quote: The tetrad was found by asking, 'What general, verifiable (that is, testable) statements can be made about all media?' We were surprised to find only four, here posed as questions
notes.claim: The McLuhans explicitly claimed the four laws were found by asking for verifiable, testable statements about all media — so the testability claim is the authors', not a publisher's or a critic's.

notes.quote: The tetrad - the four laws considered together as a cluster - is an instrument for revealing and predicting the dynamics of situations and innovations
notes.claim: McLuhan's own predictive claim for the tetrad: it is an instrument for revealing AND predicting the dynamics of situations and innovations — which undercuts the reading that the fourth law is not a forecast.

report.body:
## TL;DR

McLuhan's tetrad claims every artefact simultaneously enhances something, obsolesces something, retrieves something older, and reverses into something else when pushed to its limit — a universal, non-chronological grammar of technological effect [20][1]. The McLuhans presented it as "verifiable (that is, testable) statements" about all media [20], then defended it as a heuristic when critics took the claim seriously [3][15]. Scholarship since 1988 has used the tetrad as an interpretive and teaching device, extending it to environments, users and non-human objects, while its most careful users treat it as a probe that cannot be falsified [2][3][13]. No study located for this report tested it empirically, and the one place a quadrant meets real data — whether games displace television — the studies disagree [3]. It is very likely the tetrad cannot be tested in its own terms, since its tradition presents it as non-causal and myth-like [21].

## Key Findings

- The four laws are enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal, and in the McLuhans' own words all four operate at once rather than in sequence: "All four aspects are inherent in each artifact from the start" [20].
- The scope claimed was universal and checkable. The four were found by asking "What general, verifiable (that is, testable) statements can be made about all media?" [20], and Eric McLuhan claimed the answers could be checked "by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [3].
- McLuhan also claimed predictive force, calling the tetrad "an instrument for revealing and predicting the dynamics of situations and innovations" [20] — a stronger claim than most of his defenders now make.
- The McLuhans' own practice contradicts the checkability claim: two different tetrads for wine on the same page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206) [3].
- Tom Tyler's critique is a double bind, not a vagueness complaint: the tetrad is too loose to falsify ("a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things") and too rigid to be honest ("it _requires_ us to fill the gaps") [3].
- Tyler's verdict: calling these scientific laws in any ordinary sense is "preposterous", but "the tetrad has its uses" as a probe [3].
- Robert Logan, McLuhan's collaborator, concedes the laws "are not strictly scientific laws" because a tetrad makes no unique prediction and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions" [2].
- Named extensions exist: Laws of Media Environments and Laws of Media Users (Iseri and Logan) [2]; tetrads of human-made, animal-made and natural screens following Harman [14]; and Logan's own reversal in which users become extensions of their media [22].
- Applied tetrads are common and mostly assert rather than test: on the smartphone [8], on telemedicine during Covid-19 [9], on Microsoft Teams, and as "testing heuristics" in software testing [12].
- The nearest thing to an empirical test is Tyler's treatment of obsolescence as displacement. The Kaiser Family Foundation found heavy users of one medium are heavy users of others; Nick Yee found players displacing television. Tyler: "existing studies are collectively uncertain" [3].
- The second law resists testing by design, because Tyler redefines obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction — after which no survivorship data can count against it [3].
- No inter-coder reliability study, prediction ledger or falsification attempt was located. In the media-ecology account of the method, the tetrad is arrived at by expert judgment from the analyst's "historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject" [21].
- The tradition's own account explains why. Hempell describes the tetrad as "an alternate means for discussing the effect of technology on society" rather than "a model based on causality" [21], and quotes McLuhan and Powers on a tetrad that performs "the function of myth" [21].
- The political-economy and decolonial objections target the framework's silence on power: without a political dimension the analysis "quickly collapses into a strictly cultural one" [7], and the global village "failed to account for the power dynamics" [7].
- The tetrad also cannot say whose effects it is counting. Disability research locates effects in an interaction between a person and a built environment, and finds them distributed unevenly — disabled New Zealand internet users had "restricted fibre access and higher wireless broadband" [18].

## Details

### 1. What the four laws actually claim, and what status the McLuhans claimed for them

Marshall McLuhan proposed the four "laws of media" in the mid-1970s, describing them as "a rigorous means of investigating" the effects of artefacts on people and society [3]. The four were collected in book form in *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988), written with his son Eric McLuhan [3]. The laws take the form of four questions asked of any artefact: what does it enhance or intensify; what does it obsolesce or displace; what does it retrieve that was previously obsolesced; and what does it become when pressed to an extreme [20]. Tyler's summary of the radio case shows how the quadrants were meant to interlock: radio amplifies the voice to "simultaneous access to the entire planet", obsolesces print as the vehicle of breaking news, retrieves the town crier, and reverses into television [3].

Three features of the claim matter more than the labels. First, the four effects were said to operate at once rather than in sequence. In the McLuhans' words, the tetrad "presents not a sequential process, but rather four simultaneous ones. All four aspects are inherent in each artifact from the start" [20]. Library and Archives Canada's curatorial account stresses the same point, noting that although "McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order" [1]. Tyler likewise cites *Laws of Media* page 99 for the simultaneity of the four laws [3].

Second, the scope claimed was universal. The McLuhans say the four were found by asking "What general, verifiable (that is, testable) statements can be made about all media?" and that they "were surprised to find only four" [20]. Schumann, summarising the book, reports that McLuhan held the four laws "valid for all the artifacts of man and challenged all to find counter examples" [20]. That challenge is the hinge of the whole later debate, because it converts a descriptive vocabulary into a claim that could in principle fail.

Third, the status claimed is not one thing. In the book the McLuhans disclaim an underlying theory: "We propose no underlying theory to attack or defend, but rather a heuristic device, a set of four questions, which we call a tetrad", adding that the four questions can be asked, and the answers checked, by anyone anywhere at any time about any human artefact [20]. But the same passage continues into a claim of verifiability, and the book's subtitle calls the project a new science. The disclaimer is of a theory, not of testability. Tyler treats the checkability sentence as Eric McLuhan's own reproducibility claim, quoting it from *Laws of Media* page 7 [3].

That reproducibility claim is what the McLuhans' own practice contradicts. On a single page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206) they give two different tetrads for wine [3]. The first has wine enhancing "grape juice" through fermentation, obsolescing "commonplace flavours", retrieving "ritual observance", and reversing into "cooking wine vinegar". The second has it enhancing food and "the occasion", obsolescing "inhibition", retrieving "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reversing into "hangover" and insult [3]. Tyler's inference is that "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [3]. The answers were not, in practice, checkable by anyone anywhere.

A fourth claim sits alongside these: that the tetrad predicts. McLuhan calls it "an instrument for revealing and predicting the dynamics of situations and innovations" [20]. That is a stronger claim than the media-ecology reading allows, and it is what makes the absence of any predictive record (section 4) consequential rather than merely an omission. It also sits awkwardly with McLuhan's reported rule against forecasting, which Tyler quotes as "Never predict anything that hasn't already happened" [3].

The curatorial literature reads the tension the other way. Library and Archives Canada's exhibition, which attributes its wording to *Laws of Media* page 116 and to Robert Babe's book, says the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool", but a device for exploring the grammar and syntax of an artefact and describing "situations that are in process" [1]. The same page describes the laws as pedagogical instruments, "meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [1]. So the divergence is not between McLuhan and his archivists; it is inside *Laws of Media* itself, between the passage that claims testable statements about all media and the passage that disclaims a scientific instrument.

The fourth law is the most distinctive content, and it departs from McLuhan's predecessor Harold Innis. As the archive's account notes, citing Babe, the fourth law — that an artefact reverses into an opposing form when it is overheated — "marks a significant departure from Innis" [1]. The McLuhan circle's later defence adopts the heuristic reading outright: in a *Canadian Journal of Communication* article co-authored by Eric McLuhan, a probe "is not a thing but a happening, an event", whose "virtue (i.e., power)" lies "in its launching and relaunchability" [15].

What the laws claim, then, is a universal, simultaneous, four-part grammar of artefactual effect, offered as verifiable statements about all media, as a prediction instrument, and as a heuristic that makes no theory-claim. Those three descriptions do not sit together, and all three are in the McLuhans' own text.

### 2. The critical reception: unfalsifiability, Procrustean rigidity, and the retreat to analogy

The sharpest critique comes from a scholar using the tetrad, not from a hostile outsider. Tom Tyler, then a senior lecturer in philosophy and culture at Oxford Brookes, published "A Procrustean Probe" in *Game Studies* in December 2008 to place digital games in their media environment. He opens by naming the danger in his own instrument. As a scientific theory, McLuhan's four "laws of media" "risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner". As a probe, this "tetrad" can "provide illuminating insights" into the effects of individual technologies [3].

Tyler's argument is a double bind, and both halves are needed to see why the tetrad resists testing. First, it is too loose: "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into", so "The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit" [3]. Second, it is too rigid: "just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps" [3]. The critique is thus not that the tetrad is vague. The same device is simultaneously under- and over-constraining: a creative analyst can produce any answer, and is obliged to produce four of them.

The evidence Tyler offers is the McLuhans' own. On a single page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206) they give two different tetrads for wine [3]. The first has wine enhancing "grape juice" through fermentation, obsolescing "commonplace flavours", retrieving "ritual observance", and reversing into "cooking wine vinegar" [3]. The second, on the same page, has it enhancing food and "the occasion", obsolescing "inhibition", retrieving "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reversing into "hangover" and insult [3]. Tyler's inference is that "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [3]. That targets Eric McLuhan's reproducibility claim directly, and it does so with the McLuhans' text rather than with a critic's reconstruction.

Tyler's verdict on the scientific claim is blunt. Calling them scientific laws in any ordinary sense of that phrase is, he writes, "preposterous". "And yet the tetrad has its uses" [3]. His salvage is the probe reading, quoting McLuhan's "I don't explain - I explore" and insisting the tetrad forces attention onto the artefact's "operation and effects" rather than the content of particular broadcasts or bottles [3]. He then sets the price of that salvage: "The diversity of results from the tetrad's application need not be a problem--once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity--so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [3]. Diversity of answers becomes a feature only if the scientific claim is abandoned.

Tyler also shows what happens when a quadrant meets real evidence. Treating obsolescence as a displacement hypothesis about television, he assembles the studies and finds them split. The Kaiser Family Foundation's panel of 8- to 18-year-olds found that heavy users of one medium are heavy users of others, so the looked-for "displacement effect" did not appear; Nick Yee's survey of massively multiplayer online players found the opposite, with 21.0 hours a week of play alongside 7.7 hours of television against a national average near 28 [3]. Tyler's conclusion is that "existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [3]. He then rescues the quadrant by redefining it: obsolescence is not extinction, since newspapers did not die out with radio, "any more than "commonplace flavours" disappeared with the consumption of wine" [3]. The redefinition is reasonable, and it also removes the second law from empirical reach, because a claim that a medium displaces a function without replacing it is compatible with any survivorship data.

Sympathetic users concede much of the same ground. Robert K. Logan, McLuhan's collaborator at Toronto, writes that "LOMs are not strictly scientific laws", because "a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into", and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [2]. The anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, applying the tetrad to the Internet, calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" but treats them as a usable first cut that "needs supplementing" before it yields "a more accurate reflection" [13].

Two critiques attack the framework's scope rather than its logic. The political-economy objection, as Library and Archives Canada's exhibition summarises it, is that without a political dimension the analysis "quickly collapses into a strictly cultural one, bereft of an account of how capital and power operate within a globalized structure" [7]. The decolonial objection is that "his valorization of oral culture is often Orientalist and romantic", and that McLuhan's global village "failed to account for the power dynamics in a globalized media environment" [7]. The wider field-level version of that charge, from Last Moyo, is that media and communication studies "lie at the centre of Euro-American modernity" and that decolonisation "must decentre Eurocentrism and imperial theories" [6]. Moyo does not discuss the tetrad, so this frames the objection rather than applying it; a four-law schema illustrated mainly with wine, radio and television is exactly the kind of universalising apparatus the argument targets.

The counter-move comes from philosophy rather than media studies. Graham Harman argues the tetrad applies to all objects and not only human artefacts, since every object is a medium; media-ecology scholars took that up explicitly, treating human-made, animal-made and natural screens as media in an article that "takes this framework in considering the screen as medium" [14]. Harman's reading makes the tetrad more metaphysical, not more testable. Both sides of that disagreement accept that it is not ordinary empirical science.

### 3. Applications and extensions: tetrad wheels, digital media, and applied tetrads

The most common use of the tetrad is as an interpretive frame applied to one new medium at a time. A 2016 article in *Glocality* runs the four questions on the smartphone and concludes that the tetrad "is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments" [8]. Its reversal quadrant looks forward to augmented reality and Google Glass, and it concedes that multiple readings are unavoidable, since an interpretation of the tetrad "is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [8]. The same author closes by declining to settle anything: "one cannot say with certainty what McLuhan would say about the smartphone", and the tetrad offers "an understanding and interpretation" rather than a finding [8].

Applied tetrads have travelled well beyond North American media examples. An Indonesian communication journal applied the four laws to telemedicine during Covid-19 by reviewing 23 international journals published between 2015 and 2020 [9]. Its reversal quadrant is the most substantive part of the exercise: telemedicine "appears to provide equal opportunities for everyone to get health services but when pushed to the limit of its potential, telemedicine can only have an optimal impact on good communicator, digital divide, and financial capability" [9]. That is the fourth law used to register inequality, which is more than the framework is usually asked to do.

Trade and professional practice is a separate stream. Michael Bolton, a software-testing consultant, recast the four laws as four "testing heuristics" in *Better Software* in October 2007, asking what a feature or an organisational change enhances, obsolesces, retrieves and reverses into [12]. The move is characteristic of the practitioner literature: the tetrad is borrowed as a checklist for anticipating effects, with no claim to truth.

Three named extensions go further. The first is Iseri and Logan's, which "extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU)" alongside the original Laws of Media, so that environments and users each get their own four quadrants rather than appearing only as the object of a medium's effects [2]. The second is the Harman-inspired extension to non-human-made artefacts, which produced tetrads of human-made, animal-made and natural screens, treating the tetrad as a way of knowing rather than a predictive law and arguing that the wider application strengthens it [14]. The third is comparative: a 2013 article in *Explorations in Media Ecology* merges the tetrad with Claude Lévi-Strauss's canonical formula for myth, on the ground that both are four-part figure-ground structures [10]. Sandstrom's presentation of the method makes the extension programme explicit. McLuhan, he writes, prescribed the four effects as a complement to Aristotle's four causes, and "The invitation is to try them out on your own terms and topics" [10].

Logan's own peer-reviewed application to digital media shows the style at full stretch. Digital media, he writes, "enhance interactivity, access to information, and two-way communication", "obsolesce mass media, such as television and newspapers", "retrieve community", and "pushed far enough, they flip or reverse into hyperreality or the loss of contact with nature and our bodies" [22]. He then proposes a reversal the McLuhans did not: with digital media the direction of extension inverts, and the user becomes an extension of the medium, because "every key stroke and choice they make is information that is fed into that Big Data system" [22]. He draws on Rushkoff's account of captology and on McLuhan's own 1969 line that "The more the data banks record about each one of us, the less we exist" [22]. This is the strongest form of the extension literature: a new quadrant answer, argued from a mechanism, in a peer-reviewed journal.

Two reference works anchor the applied tradition. *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan* (2017) collects unpublished tetrads with an index, including a chapter on tetrad development and submissions that documents how the McLuhans solicited tetrads from others [19]. Library and Archives Canada's exhibition carries the same teaching material, including the standard exercise "Can you apply the laws of media to the cellular telephone?" [19].

What this literature does not contain is a case where applying the tetrad changed a conclusion. Tyler's own application is the partial exception, because he uses quadrants to attack named misconceptions: Berger's claim that solo gaming is alienating, the assumption that games displace television, the "immersive fallacy" of inevitable total immersion, and the idea of the magic circle as a sealed realm [3]. His result is deliberately modest, "one amongst many possible surveys", and his closing line states the standard he is working to: "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting investigation is ultimately constructive" [3]. Almost all other applications assert the four answers and stop.

The pattern across 40 years is therefore stable. The tetrad is used to organise an argument about a new medium, to teach a method, or to license a prediction about where a medium is heading. It is rarely used to put a proposition at risk.

### 4. Has anyone tried to test it empirically?

No study located for this report has tested the tetrad as a hypothesis. Searches for reliability studies, experimental validation, coding schemes and predictive tests returned applications of the four laws to new media, not tests of them. Four decades after *Laws of Media*, the framework has no measured inter-coder agreement, no scored prediction record and no published attempt at falsification. That is a finding about the literature, not about the tetrad's truth; it means the claim has gone unexamined rather than been refuted.

The nearest thing to a test is Tyler's treatment of the second law. If a medium obsolesces something, the effect should be visible as displacement, and Tyler assembles the studies that would show it [3]. The Kaiser Family Foundation's surveys of 8- to 18-year-olds found that heavy users of one medium tend to be heavy users of others, so the expected "displacement effect" did not appear [3]. Nick Yee's survey of massively multiplayer players found the opposite, reporting 21.0 hours a week of play against 7.7 hours of television, a total close to the national average for television alone, which Yee read as support for displacement [3]. Tyler's conclusion is that "existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [3]. That is the only place found where a quadrant is checked against conflicting measurements and reported as unresolved.

Even that falls short of a test, for a reason Tyler himself supplies. The McLuhans did not claim one medium replaces another, and Tyler redefines obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction, noting McLuhan's point that more handwriting is done daily now than before printing [3]. Once obsolescence means "repurposed" rather than "displaced", no survivorship data can count against it. A hypothesis that any outcome confirms is not being tested.

The form a test would take is not exotic. Reliability comes first: give independent analysts the same artefact and a written protocol, and measure whether their four answers agree. The McLuhans' two wine tetrads on one page suggest they would not [3]. Prediction comes second: state in advance which practice a new medium will displace or retrieve, by when, and score the outcomes. Reversal makes this harder, because McLuhan's rule was never to predict anything that has not already happened [3], and Hempell's account of the method has the analyst working from "historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject" with no coding rules or comparison case [21]. Mechanism comes third, and no one has attempted it.

Adjacent fields show what the measurement would look like. The WebAIM Million audits one million home pages each year with a fixed automated engine, detecting 56,114,377 distinct accessibility errors in its February 2026 sample, an average of 56.1 per page, and reports that "95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures", up from 94.8% in 2025 [16]. It also states the limit of its own instrument: "Absence of detected errors does not indicate that a page is accessible or conformant" [16]. That is the discipline a falsifiable tetrad would need. A stated denominator, a fixed procedure and an explicit statement of non-detection are all missing from the tetrad literature.

The same is true of the disaggregation question the tetrad never asks. A tetrad answers at the level of "society", so it cannot say whose enhancement or obsolescence is being counted. Disability scholarship locates the effect in "a built environment and organized social activity that preclude or restrict the participation of people seen or labeled as having disabilities", which makes the unit of analysis interactional rather than social [5]. The WHO's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health formalises disability as a dynamic interaction between a health condition and environmental and personal factors [5]. Empirical work in that frame finds media effects distributed unevenly: Pacheco and Burgess, surveying 960 New Zealand adult internet users, found that "people with disabilities have restricted fibre access and higher wireless broadband (a much slower connection type)" and "use social media platforms less" [18]. Statistics Canada publishes comparable Canadian data on the barriers to internet access experienced by persons with disabilities [17]. These are the measurements from which a testable version of the second law, asking what a medium obsolesces and for whom, could be built. No tetrad study uses them.

The closest historical attempt at refutation was an exchange in *Technology and Culture* rather than a study. McLuhan published "McLuhan's Laws of the Media" there in 1975, and William Henry Venable replied in 1976 with "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws", with McLuhan responding. Those three items exist and are the standard citation for a sustained critique, but the full texts were not readable here, so their content is not reported.

Why the gap has persisted is partly internal to the framework. Hempell's media-ecology account describes the tetrad as deliberately non-causal: McLuhan "proposed the tetrad as an alternate means for discussing the effect of technology on society", organising an artefact as a "resonating interval" instead of using "a model based on causality" [21]. On that reading there is nothing to test, because no causal claim is made. McLuhan and Powers go further, describing a tetrad that "performs the function of myth in that it compresses past, present, and future into one through the power of simultaneity" [21]. A framework that presents itself as myth and explicitly refuses causality cannot be falsified, and asking for its error rate is a category mistake. The unexamined claim is therefore a consequence of a decision the tradition made about what kind of thing the tetrad is.

### 5. What a test would require, and where the tetrad's status now stands

The tetrad's defenders and its sharpest critic end in the same place, and the position is more defensible than either the "new science" claim or the "preposterous" verdict suggests. The tetrad is a generative instrument whose four answers are hypotheses to be argued for, quadrant by quadrant, against evidence. Logan states the reason it cannot be more: a tetrad makes no unique prediction about what will be retrieved or what a medium will flip into, and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions" [2]. Eriksen states the condition of use: the laws are overambitious and deterministic, and the model can be "a starting-point (although it needs supplementing)" [13]. Tyler states the test of quality: diversity of answers is acceptable only "once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity" and only where the results provide "illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [3].

Read that way, the quality of a tetrad turns on properties that can be checked even though the tetrad as a whole cannot be falsified. Does each quadrant name a concrete practice rather than an abstraction like "ritual"? Is there evidence cited per quadrant, and is contrary evidence reported? Are the terms defined, so that obsolescence means remediation and reversal means potential already visible? Are the two dualisms that generate the four boxes stated, in Harman's sense, so that the fourfold is not merely decoration [14]? Is each quadrant aimed at a specific misconception, as Tyler's are? Are rival tetrads generated and compared, as the McLuhans failed to do with wine? Does anything follow that could embarrass the analyst?

Those criteria also set what would count as progress. A reliability study would measure whether independent analysts, given a written protocol, converge on the same four answers; the two wine tetrads predict they would not [3]. A prediction ledger would date and score each forward claim; the fourth law's exclusion of forecasts [3] means only claims about potential already realised could be scored. A disaggregated version would answer the second law per population rather than for society, which existing disability and access statistics could support [18]. None of the three has been done.

No published study located for this report tested the tetrad, and its own practitioners describe the method as unstructured expert judgment [21]. The evidence is therefore consistent with the tetrad never having been subjected to a formal empirical test, but it cannot establish that none exists anywhere; a null result from keyword searching is weak evidence. The framework probably cannot be tested in its own terms, because the tradition presents it as non-causal and myth-like [21]. That is an inference from the sources' own descriptions, not a measured finding. What the evidence shows is narrower and more useful: the tetrad's four questions reliably generate candidate effects, and it has no procedure for deciding which candidates are real.

The claim that the tetrad is "not meant to be a scientific tool" [1] is now the mainstream reading, including in the institutions that curate McLuhan's papers. That reading rescues the framework from Tyler's charge by giving up the thing the McLuhans themselves asserted in 1975 and 1988. The cost is that nothing follows from a tetrad that could not equally have been said without it — which is the position most of the applied literature is in, and the reason its four boxes so rarely overturn anything.


## Beyond this question

Anyone applying the tetrad now works under a claim their own tradition has abandoned. The McLuhans asserted testable statements about all media and a predictive instrument [20]; the settled reading, including in the institutions that curate the papers, is that the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool" [1]. That gap has a practical cost, because the four questions will always return four answers. Tyler's double bind is the operating constraint: the device is loose enough to fit anything and rigid enough to demand a fit [3].

Three habits follow from the evidence. Generate rival tetrads rather than one, since the McLuhans' failure with wine was not producing two but publishing them as though either would be reproduced [3]. Leave a quadrant empty when the evidence is absent, rather than filling it for symmetry. And convert each quadrant's claim into something that could fail: a named practice displaced, a named practice retrieved, a date by which it would be visible. Logan's concession that a tetrad makes no unique prediction [2] is the reason the answers must be argued rather than asserted.

The disaggregation problem is the largest untapped extension. A tetrad answers for "society", which cannot say whose enhancement or obsolescence is being counted [5]. Statistics Canada already publishes the barrier data that would let the second law be answered per population [17], and survey work shows media effects falling unevenly across disabled and non-disabled users [18]. Nobody has run a tetrad that way.

For anyone treating the tetrad as a design or foresight tool, as the practitioner literature does [12], the honest label is ideation heuristic. That is not a demotion: it is what the applied literature actually delivers, and it stops the four boxes being mistaken for findings.

## Open questions

- **Whether any formal test exists.** No study located for this report tested the tetrad, but keyword searching cannot prove a negative. A citation search forward from *Laws of Media* in a subscription database would settle it; that was not available here.
- **Whether reliability is measurable.** Nobody has given independent analysts a written protocol and measured agreement on the four quadrants. The two wine tetrads predict low agreement [3], but that is a prediction, not a result.
- **What the 1975–76 exchange actually argued.** McLuhan's "McLuhan's Laws of the Media" (1975) and Venable's "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (1976) in *Technology and Culture* are the standard citation for a sustained critique. The full texts were not readable here, so this report does not say what they argued. This is the largest gap in the coverage.
- **Whether the tetrad's dualisms hold up.** Harman's test — that a rigorous fourfold must cross two profound dualisms — was reported here from the record rather than from his chapter read in full, so his argument is summarised at second hand.
- **What the fourth law can be scored against.** McLuhan claimed the tetrad predicts [20] and also said never to predict anything that has not already happened [3]. Until that is resolved, reversal cannot be tested even in principle.
- **Whether any application has changed a conclusion.** Tyler's is the only case found where quadrants were used to overturn named misconceptions [3]. Whether the applied literature has ever revised an author's view is unmeasured.
- **Independence of the critical case.** Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe" carries most of the negative argument here, in both its DiGRA 2007 and *Game Studies* 2008 versions, and those two texts overlap almost word for word. They count as one voice, not two. No second independent critique of comparable rigour was read in full, so the double-bind reading of the tetrad rests on one scholar's analysis plus the McLuhans' text.
- **Coverage.** Three sources in this report come from one government exhibition page, and the media-ecology material is thin: Hempell's paper is a practitioner essay, and the *Explorations in Media Ecology* items on the tetrad and phenomenology and on the "missing media laws" could not be read. The evidence on testing is therefore mostly a well-documented absence rather than a survey of attempts.
