sentences.sentence: Statistics Canada found that "In 2013, 50% of employees aged 15 to 19 and 13% of those aged 20 to 24 were paid at minimum wage" [2].
Statistics Canada's own survey of the evidence is narrower: "In Canada, the effects of an increase in the minimum wage on total employment would typically be small or non-existent" [2].

Statistics Canada treats "the ratio of the minimum wage to the average hourly earnings" as the conditioning variable, and reports that "when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant" [2].

Dube and Reich argue exactly this about the opposing literature, reporting that its results are "confounded by 1990s-era parallel trends violations amplified by the two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) model" [6].
Second, a credible finding of *positive* youth employment effects would undercut it, since that requires employer wage-setting power strong enough to reverse the sign [21].

Third, a null result is not automatically a refutation: as one synthesis puts it, "Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective" [21].

For scale, the pre-2017 Canadian literature puts the teen elasticity between about −0.1 and −0.4 — a calculation from [10], which reports a 1%–4% reduction in teen employment rates for a 10% minimum wage increase.
A meta-analysis of that literature centres it at −0.27 [3].

Official "minimum wage" counts include workers legally paid below the general rate and workers not covered by the law: "Hourly earnings below the established minimum do not necessarily indicate an infringement of the law" [15].

The Labour Force Survey that produces these figures samples "approximately 56,000 Canadian households for individuals aged 15 years and over" [14] and excludes the territories, people on reserves and people in institutions [15].
Applying meta-regression to test for selective reporting, it finds the literature is not distorted by publication bias and estimates a teenage employment elasticity of about −0.27 [3].

They found that "The results indicate that the minimum wage increases have increased the transition from employment to non-employment of employed low-wage youths" by around 6 percentage points, implying elasticities of about −0.4, with a range of −0.3 to −0.5 [5].

Their conclusion was that "Our minimum wage elasticities are substantial, typically in the range of −0.14 to −0.44, with −0.30 being a reasonable point estimate," and, importantly, that the effects were larger after lagged adjustment [8].

A panel study across Canadian provinces from 1981 to 2011, using many provincial amendments, reports that its ordinary least squares and instrumental variables estimates "imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" and it also found lower employment among prime-aged immigrants [10].
First, Statistics Canada's own analysts state that "The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States" [2].

Second, the mechanism is one of hiring rather than firing, which means conventional headcount series understate it: "For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group" [2].

Reviewing the entire subnational literature, they conclude that "there is a clear preponderance of negative estimates in the literature" and that the evidence is stronger for teens and young adults and for the less-educated [13].

Neumark and Wascher's earlier monograph made the same claim in stronger terms: "A sizable majority of the studies surveyed in this monograph give a relatively consistent (although not always statistically significant) indication of negative employment effects of minimum wages" [9].
The United Kingdom sets youth minimum wage rates far below the adult rate: £5.28 for 16 to 17 year olds and £7.49 for 18 to 20 year olds against £10.42 for those 23 and over in April 2023 [17].
Canadian provinces mostly apply the full adult rate to teenagers, and the federal minimum wage database notes that special categories such as a student rate exist "in two provinces" only [19].

The Low Pay Commission also retains an explicit escape clause, able to advise the government to review its target "If the economic evidence warrants it" [17] — a safeguard no Canadian province has built into its uprating.

The strongest international evidence for the thesis is youth-specific and comes from age-threshold designs, and it is weighed in section 3 rather than here because it arrives with the counter-case's own source: in Denmark a 40 per cent minimum wage rise at age 18 cut employment among 18-year-olds by 33 per cent [22].

Those designs identify the effect off a discontinuity at a birthday, which sidesteps the pre-trend dispute that divides the US literature [6][7].\n\nThe case for, in sum, rests on a Canadian literature that is unusually consistent for economics: a meta-analysis free of detectable publication bias at −0.27 [3], a flows study at about −0.4 [5], a pre-specified design at −0.30 [8], and a four-decade panel implying 1% to 4% per 10% [10].

One body of international evidence does not fit this case and is weighed here rather than omitted: where a minimum wage rises sharply at a specific age, youth job losses are large and precisely estimated [22].

Its conclusion is direct: "Overall the most up to date body of research from US, UK and other developed countries points to a very muted effect of minimum wages on employment, while significantly increasing the earnings of low paid workers." It adds: "Importantly, this was found to be the case even for the most recent ambitious policies" [1].
The strongest single study behind that conclusion is Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer's analysis of US state minimum wage changes from 1979 to 2016 [4].

Its finding is precise: "We find that the overall number of low-wage jobs remained essentially unchanged over five years following the increase." Wage gains were amplified by spillovers up the distribution [4].

Crucially, the authors tested and rejected the obvious escape route for the thesis — that job losses are hidden by reshuffling: "Our estimates by detailed demographic groups show that the lack of job loss is not explained by labor-labor substitution at the bottom of the wage distribution" [4].

Employers in low-wage labour markets have wage-setting power, so a higher floor can reduce vacancies and turnover rather than headcount: "In an imperfectly competitive labour market, a higher minimum wage could reduce vacancies and turnover instead of destroying jobs" [1].

Exactly how far one can push the minimum wage before job losses start becoming pronounced is an empirical question" [1] — but the monopsony model means a null result is a prediction of theory, not an anomaly.
When using data from the last 25 years (the period with most state-level minimum wage variation), different methodologies tend to be much more in accordance with each other" [1].

Dube and Zipperer's later compilation of 88 studies puts the median own-wage elasticity at −0.13 across 72 journal-published studies, and notes that "Estimates published since 2010 tend to be closer to zero" [26].
Wolfson's 2024 study turns to Canada explicitly because it has "too few clusters for conventional clustering techniques to be reliable" and applies inference robust to few clusters [25].
It "detects no such response" — no long-run employment response to minimum wages [25].

Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute, evaluating annual minimum wage rises from 2016 to 2025 with difference-in-differences, reports: "We find no evidence that recent minimum wage increases in Ireland increased the likelihood of minimum wage employees losing their jobs" [20].
It states plainly that "we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls" [24].

Using HMRC payroll data by region for 2023 to 2025, it found the reverse: "we find the opposite – youth employment fell more in areas with the lowest youth coverage and the largest falls in youth employee numbers have been in London where youth coverage is low" [24].

The rival explanation for falling youth employment is sectoral, and the Commission states it: "Hospitality and retail are particularly important as they are the largest employers of young people" [24].

This is a live alternative for Canada too, where the same two sectors dominate minimum-wage employment — Statistics Canada reports 17% of retail employees and 27% of food and accommodation employees at the minimum in 2013 [16].

First, Irish evidence shows employers adjust on hours rather than headcount, with effects "strongest in the industry and accommodation and food sectors" [22] — so a null on separations is not a null on youth employment.

Second, the ESRI's own data contain a youth-specific negative result in the earlier period: sub-minimum youth workers who had a birthday and aged into a higher wage band "were 15 percentage points more likely to enter non-employment", though the authors caution the result rests on "a relatively small sample size" [20].
The ESRI's own review sets Dube (2019) against Neumark and Shirley (2022) on this question [22].

Kreiner and co-authors find that turning 18 in Denmark, which triggers a 40 per cent minimum wage increase, "led to a 33 per cent drop in employment and a 45 per cent reduction in hours worked among 18-year-olds" [22].
In the Netherlands, Kabátek finds employers "are more likely to lay off young workers in the three months preceding their birthday, upon which their wage entitlements would increase" [22].

These designs identify the effect off a discontinuity in the wage at a birthday rather than off cross-province variation, so they are not exposed to the pre-trend problem that divides the US literature [6][7].
The ESRI, which reports them, is the same source that finds no Irish job loss [20], so it cannot be dismissed as a partisan selection.
The Low Pay Commission reports that "the bite of the youth minimum wages (the ratio of the NMW to median hourly earnings) remains below the levels seen prior to 2016" [18].

Statistics Canada states the conditioning variable directly: "An important indicator of how increases in the minimum wage affect employment is the ratio of the minimum wage to the average hourly earnings (AHE)" [2].
Its analysts put a number on where the effect starts to matter: "when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant" [2].
Dube's review gives the matching benchmark from US data: "the employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage", and even "up to 81% of the median wage" in low-wage counties [1].

The Low Pay Commission reports that despite large nominal increases, "the bite of the youth minimum wages (the ratio of the NMW to median hourly earnings) remains below the levels seen prior to 2016", and youth coverage "remains below 2019 levels" [18].

Dube and Reich argue the negative findings are an artefact: the opposing results are "confounded by 1990s-era parallel trends violations amplified by the two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) model, which is also unreliable for detecting such violations", and "With post-2000 data, JNR’s specification does not indicate substantial disemployment" [6].

Neumark and co-authors reply that the null findings depend on the comparison geography: "Using the same research design, we show that this result is overturned if we use instead multi-state commuting zones, which provide superior definitions of local economic areas", and that the county-pair design is biased positive [7].
Statistics Canada's own footnote states that "The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States", citing Gunderson (2008) and Fortin (2010) [2].
The Canadian teen estimate discussed in section 2 sits well away from the international median Dube and Zipperer report across 72 journal-published studies [26].

The effect on teenagers works through hiring, not firing: "For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group" [2].
The ESRI result on hours rather than headcount points the same way [22].

Inference: the quantity that would resolve it is the provincial minimum-wage-to-average-earnings ratio for 2017 to 2024, set against youth employment flows in provinces that crossed the StatCan threshold at different times [2].
Every Canadian study in the case for section 2 is estimated on data ending in 1997 or 2011 [5][8][10][3].

Dube and Reich's central methodological claim is that estimates from those decades are the least reliable, because they come from a period of little cross-state variation and are contaminated by pre-trend violations [6].

The test is runnable: the federal Minimum Wage Database provides province-by-province general minimum wage rates back to 1965 and "allows for a customized search, by jurisdiction, for general minimum wage rates" [19], and the Labour Force Survey provides monthly youth employment by province [14].

The thesis is conditional on the ratio of the minimum wage to average earnings, and Dube's review sets the threshold at "around 59% of the median wage" for small effects [1], while Statistics Canada puts the point of significance near 50% of average hourly earnings [2].
As one synthesis puts it, "Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective" [21].
Neumark and Wascher state the falsification standard plainly: "we see very few - if any - studies that provide convincing evidence of positive employment effects of minimum wages" [9].
The monopsony model allows for it [1], and this review found no Canadian youth estimate of that kind.
The UK Low Pay Commission ran the geographic version of this test and the thesis failed it: youth employment fell most where youth minimum-wage coverage was lowest [24].

The UK has a standing Low Pay Commission that publishes ex ante estimates of "the likely number of jobs affected" for each uprating [23], and retains an explicit power to advise the government to review its target "If the economic evidence warrants it" [17].

Dube's own recommendation to the UK government — that more ambitious minimum wages be accompanied by "a clear mandate that the Low Pay Commission (LPC) can use to implement, evaluate and recalibrate any proposed changes" [1] — describes precisely the machinery Canada lacks.

Neumark and Wascher argue that apparent publication bias in this literature is better read as a real change in the estimated effect over time: "the evidence is more consistent with a change in the estimated minimum wage effect over time than with publication bias" [12].

notes.quote: Overall the most up to date body of research from US, UK and other developed countries points to a very muted effect of minimum wages on employment, while significantly increasing the earnings of low paid workers. Importantly, this was found to be the case even for the most recent ambitious policies.
notes.claim: Dube's UK Treasury-commissioned review of the international evidence concludes that the weight of modern research finds a very muted employment effect from minimum wages even for ambitious recent increases — the central counter-case to the thesis.

notes.quote: In an imperfectly competitive labour market, a higher minimum wage could reduce vacancies and turnover instead of destroying jobs. Of course, eventually a higher minimum wage will lower employment. Exactly how far one can push the minimum wage before job losses start becoming pronounced is an empirical question.
notes.claim: The monopsony/turnover rival explanation: firms have wage-setting power, so a higher minimum can cut vacancies and turnover rather than jobs, making zero job loss theoretically coherent.

notes.quote: The extent of the effect on employment depends on a number of factors,Note 4 including the ratio of the minimum wage to the average hourly earnings (AHE). The higher this ratio—that is, the closer the minimum wage to average hourly earnings (all things being equal)—the more workers are affected by minimum wage legislation and the greater the effects on employment.
notes.claim: The "bite" of the minimum wage is measured as the ratio of the minimum wage to average hourly earnings; the thesis is implicitly conditional on this ratio rising substantially, which is how the 2017+ provincial increases are argued to matter.

notes.quote: In Canada, the effects of an increase in the minimum wage on total employment would typically be small or non-existent.Note 2 Rather, an increase in the minimum wage would seem to be associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers,Note 3 who are most likely to be paid at this hourly rate.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's Labour Statistics Division frames the thesis narrowly: aggregate employment effects are "small or non-existent," with disemployment concentrated among teenagers, the group most likely to be paid the minimum. This is the version of the claim the report should test (youth-specific, not total employment).

notes.quote: I find no evidence of a publication bias and a minimum wage elasticity of about −0.27
notes.claim: Campolieti's meta-analysis of Canadian minimum-wage studies (Canadian Public Policy, 46(4), 2020) finds no publication bias for teenagers and a teenage employment elasticity of about -0.27 — roughly a 2.7% fall in teen employment per 10% minimum-wage rise. This is the central Canadian quantitative estimate in the case for youth job losses.

notes.quote: An important indicator of how increases in the minimum wage affect employment is the ratio of the minimum wage to the average hourly earnings (AHE).
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's own analysts treat the minimum-wage-to-average-hourly-earnings ratio (the "bite") as the key conditioning variable for whether a minimum wage increase affects employment — the crux is not the wage level but this ratio.

notes.quote: In 2013, 50% of employees aged 15 to 19 and 13% of those aged 20 to 24 were paid at minimum wage.
notes.claim: By 2013 half of employed 15-19 year olds were paid at exactly the minimum wage, showing that teens are overwhelmingly the directly affected group and that coverage (share at the wage floor) is the measure of bite that matters for youth.

notes.quote: We find that the overall number of low-wage jobs remained essentially unchanged over five years following the increase. At the same time, the direct effect of the minimum wage on average earnings was amplified by modest wage spillovers at the bottom of the wage distribution. Our estimates by detailed demographic groups show that the lack of job loss is not explained by labor-labor substitution at the bottom of the wage distribution.
notes.claim: Cengiz-Dube-Lindner-Zipperer bunching study of 138 US state minimum wage changes 1979-2016: low-wage job counts essentially unchanged over five years, wage gains amplified by spillovers, and the null is not explained by labour-labour substitution.

notes.quote: The results indicate that the minimum wage increases have increased the transition from employment to non-employment of employed low-wage youths, who are at-risk of being affected by a minimum wage increase, by around 6 percentage points (ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points). These disemployment effects in turn imply ‘minimum wage’ elasticities of about −0.4 (ranging from −0.3 to −0.5).
notes.claim: Campolieti, Fang and Gunderson (Canadian Journal of Economics, 2005), using SLID longitudinal data and 24 provincial minimum-wage changes in the 1990s, find that minimum-wage increases raised the employment-to-non-employment transition of low-wage youths by about 6 percentage points (4 to 8), implying elasticities of about -0.4 (range -0.3 to -0.5).

notes.quote: According to Brochu and Green (2012), when the minimum wage is high, labour market transitions (hirings and layoffs) tend to decrease. For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group.
notes.claim: The crux mechanism identified by StatCan: the effect on youth shows up in hiring flows rather than layoffs, which means stock measures of employment understate the effect — a measurement disagreement that turns on gross flows.

notes.quote: Importantly, modern event study designs (using either MSCZs or BCPs) show no local pre-tends, and find no meaningful employment decline.
notes.claim: The Dube–Reich school's core claim: with modern event-study designs there is no meaningful employment decline from higher minimum wages, and the Neumark-style findings of disemployment are attributable to pre-existing trends confounded by the estimator. This is the main "rival explanation" the thesis must survive.

notes.quote: Using the same research design, we show that this result is overturned if we use instead multi-state commuting zones, which provide superior definitions of local economic areas. These contrasting results are explained by a positive bias in the county-pair specification when using pairs formed by counties from different commuting zones.
notes.claim: Neumark's side insists the negative finding is real and depends on the choice of local labour market definition: the county-pair design used by Dube-Lester-Reich is positively biased, and multi-state commuting zones overturn the no-effect result. The thesis's validity therefore turns partly on which comparison geography is used.

notes.quote: Our minimum wage elasticities are substantial, typically in the range of −0.14 to −0.44, with −0.30 being a reasonable point estimate, and with the effects being larger after lagged adjustments.
notes.claim: Campolieti, Gunderson and Riddell (Industrial Relations, 2006), applying Neumark's prespecified research design to Canadian data 1981-1997, find substantial elasticities of -0.14 to -0.44 with -0.30 a reasonable point estimate, and larger effects after lagged adjustment — evidence that disemployment effects grow over time rather than appearing only on impact.

notes.quote: However, the oft-stated assertion that recent research fails to support the traditional view that the minimum wage reduces the employment of low-wage workers is clearly incorrect. A sizable majority of the studies surveyed in this monograph give a relatively consistent (although not always statistically significant) indication of negative employment effects of minimum wages.
notes.claim: Neumark–Wascher's survey of the "new minimum wage research" argues the weight of studies points to negative employment effects — the standard the thesis would need to meet, and the critic's claim that the contrary literature is a minority.

notes.quote: First, we see very few - if any - studies that provide convincing evidence of positive employment effects of minimum wages, especially from those studies that focus on the broader groups (rather than a narrow industry) for which the competitive model predicts disemployment effects.
notes.claim: States the falsification test the thesis faces: a credible study finding positive (not merely null) employment effects for a broad youth group would undercut it — and Neumark–Wascher say almost none exists.

notes.quote: Ordinary least squares and instrumental variables (IV) estimates imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens. We also find that an increase in the minimum wage is associated with lower employment of prime-aged immigrants.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed Canadian panel study (185 provincial minimum-wage amendments, 1981–2011) quantifies the thesis's magnitude for teens: a 10% minimum-wage increase associated with a 1%–4% reduction in teen employment rates. This gives the report the concrete elasticity range the thesis must be stated at.

notes.quote: We find that the negative elasticities in national fixed-effects models are generated by unobserved heterogeneities in employment trends. Our local estimators are more robust and show no employment effects.
notes.claim: Dube-Lester-Reich's founding statement of the rival interpretation: the negative teenage elasticities in national fixed-effects models are an artefact of unobserved heterogeneity in spatial employment trends, and border-county estimators show no employment effects. This is the alternative hypothesis against which a youth-loss claim must be distinguished.

notes.quote: Of course, eventually a higher minimum wage will lower employment. Exactly how far one can push the minimum wage before job losses start becoming pronounced is an empirical question.
notes.claim: Dube's review for the UK government sets the falsification condition explicitly: a minimum wage can be pushed some distance before job losses become pronounced, and where that threshold lies is an empirical question — so the thesis is testable only against a specific "bite" level.

notes.quote: Across US states, the best evidence suggests that the employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage. Evidence using sub-state county-level variation found this to hold even in lower wage counties where the minimum stood at up to 81% of the median wage.
notes.claim: Dube's review states a quantitative benchmark — US evidence finds small employment effects up to roughly 59% of the median wage — which is the number that would have to be compared with Canadian provincial minimum wages to test the thesis; it also notes counter-examples exist.

notes.quote: However, given that the evidence base is still developing, it would also be prudent to accompany more ambitious minimum wages with a clear mandate that the Low Pay Commission (LPC) can use to implement, evaluate and recalibrate any proposed changes to the NLW, thereby designing in responsiveness to any unforeseen impacts if required.
notes.claim: Dube recommends designing in a pre-committed reversal rule and better data (administrative earnings records, timely evaluation) — i.e., a concrete list of what evidence would overturn a policy conclusion, and an admission that the current evidence base is too weak to settle high-bite cases.

notes.quote: We present results indicating that the evidence is more consistent with a change in the estimated minimum wage effect over time than with publication bias. More generally, we demonstrate that existing approaches to testing for publication bias may generate spurious evidence of such bias when there are structural changes in some parameters.
notes.claim: Neumark–Wascher argue the appearance of publication bias in the minimum-wage time-series literature is better explained by a genuine change in the estimated effect over time — a direct challenge to the claim that the pro-thesis literature is an artefact of selective reporting.

notes.quote: Our key conclusions are: (i) there is a clear preponderance of negative estimates in the literature; (ii) this evidence is stronger for teens and young adults as well as the less-educated;
notes.claim: Neumark and Shirley (NBER WP 28388, 2021; published in Industrial Relations 2022) assembled the entire US subnational literature and concluded there is a clear preponderance of negative estimates, stronger for teens and young adults and the less-educated — the canonical Neumark-style reading of the evidence.

notes.quote: Every month, the LFS collects data from approximately 56,000 Canadian households for individuals aged 15 years and over, excluding full-time members of the Armed Forces, persons living on an Indian reserve, and institutional residents.
