So "minimum-wage employment" in the official data is not the same as "employment affected by the minimum wage."

notes.quote: In 2013, 50% of employees aged 15 to 19 years old were paid at minimum wage. Among those aged 20 to 24, the rate was 13%.
notes.claim: Official exposure figures locate the "bite": in 2013 half of employees aged 15-19 and 13% of those aged 20-24 were paid at the minimum wage, versus 6.7% of all paid employees, with retail (17%) and accommodation/food (27%) dominating. This is why the thesis is about young workers specifically — they are the only group the policy directly touches in large numbers.

notes.quote: Because of this labour market strength for 16-17 and 18-20 year olds we recommended increases of 9.7 per cent – in line with the increase in the NLW – for both of these groups, to £5.28 and £7.49 respectively.
notes.claim: UK Low Pay Commission: youth subminimum rates are set far below the adult rate (£5.28 for 16-17 and £7.49 for 18-20 versus £10.42 for 23+ in April 2023), and the LPC raised the youth rates only because youth employment had recovered to near pre-pandemic levels — an institutional difference that limits how far UK "no job loss" findings transfer to Canadian provinces, where 15-19 year olds typically get the full adult rate.

notes.quote: If the economic evidence warrants it, we can advise the Government to review the target or its timeframe. This ‘emergency brake’ is intended to ensure the lowest-paid workers continue to see pay rises without significant risks to their employment prospects.
notes.claim: The LPC's remit is to raise youth rates "as high as possible without damaging employment", and it retains an explicit "emergency brake" allowing it to advise reviewing the target if the economic evidence warrants — an institutional safeguard Canadian provinces lack, relevant to why the UK evidence cannot be read straight across to Canada.

notes.quote: However, JNR’s results are confounded by 1990s-era parallel trends violations amplified by the two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) model, which is also unreliable for detecting such violations. With post-2000 data, JNR’s specification does not indicate substantial disemployment.
notes.claim: This states precisely how the youth-loss thesis could be shown wrong: if the provinces that raised wages most were already on diverging youth-employment trends before 2017, the estimated loss is a pre-trend artefact. Dube-Reich attribute the opposing (Neumark-side) disemployment result to exactly this, and report that with post-2000 data the same specification shows no substantial disemployment — so the thesis lives or dies on parallel pre-trends and the sample window.

notes.quote: And the bite of the youth minimum wages (the ratio of the NMW to median hourly earnings) remains below the levels seen prior to 2016. Despite large increases in minimum wage rates, the coverage of the youth rates (for 16-20 year olds) only increased by two percentage points this year and remains below 2019 levels.
notes.claim: The UK Low Pay Commission — the institution with the longest record of phased minimum-wage increases — reports that the bite of youth rates remains below pre-2016 levels and that large increases to youth rates have produced no robust evidence of harm, i.e., the youth bite in the UK is still modest relative to Canada's.

notes.quote: For teenagers, the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators, I find no evidence of a publication bias and a minimum wage elasticity of about −0.27
notes.claim: A meta-analysis of the Canadian minimum-wage literature finds no publication bias and a teenage employment elasticity of about -0.27, far larger in magnitude than the near-zero US estimates — so the Canadian crux is that the same designs yield a bigger youth effect in Canada.

notes.quote: Using the same research design, we show that this result is overturned if we use instead multi-state commuting zones, which provide superior definitions of local economic areas. These contrasting results are explained by a positive bias in the county-pair specification when using pairs formed by counties from different commuting zones.
notes.claim: The border-discontinuity crux: Neumark and co-authors argue the Dube-Lester-Reich county-pair design is biased positive and that commuting-zone designs do find disemployment — the disagreement turns on which local labour market definition and which pre-trend handling is used.

notes.quote: Special categories with a different minimum wage can include students under the age of 18 (in two provinces) and some occupations.
notes.claim: The federal Minimum Wage Database shows that only two provinces have a separate sub-minimum student rate, and that special categories are the exception — relevant to whether Canadian data can isolate a youth-specific effect at all, since most provinces apply one adult rate to teenagers.

notes.quote: Across US states, the best evidence suggests that the employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage. Evidence using sub-state county-level variation found this to hold even in lower wage counties where the minimum stood at up to 81% of the median wage.
notes.claim: The bite threshold the whole dispute turns on: US evidence finds employment effects small up to roughly 59% of the median wage, and even up to 81% in low-wage counties — giving a benchmark against which Canadian minimum-wage bites can be judged.

notes.quote: However, JNR’s results are confounded by 1990s-era parallel trends violations amplified by the two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) model, which is also unreliable for detecting such violations. With post-2000 data, JNR’s specification does not indicate substantial disemployment.
notes.claim: Dube and co-authors reply that the disemployment findings rest on 1990s-era pre-trend violations amplified by two-way fixed effects, and that with post-2000 data and modern event studies there is no meaningful employment decline — so the crux is the pre-trend/counterfactual assumption, not the data source.

notes.quote: The database also includes past general minimum wage rates in Canada, since 1965, and allows for a customized search, by jurisdiction, for general minimum wage rates.
notes.claim: The federal database makes province-by-province minimum wages back to 1965 searchable — so the "bite" measure the thesis turns on is constructible from official data, and the test is not blocked by missing policy data.

notes.quote: We find no evidence that recent minimum wage increases in Ireland increased the likelihood of minimum wage employees losing their jobs. While minimum wage employees are generally more likely to enter non-employment than higher-paid workers, the likelihood of this happening did not increase following increases to the minimum wage.
notes.claim: Independent evaluation (ESRI, Ireland's state-funded research institute) of annual minimum wage rises 2016-2025: difference-in-differences finds no rise in job loss for minimum wage workers, and no dose-response — bigger increases did not produce more separations. A non-Canadian, non-US null result from a different institution.

notes.quote: However, there are studies that show no employment effects of minimum wages and an occasional study that shows a positive effect. Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective. Studies that show positive effects of minimum wages on youth employment are consistent with the monopsony story.
notes.claim: A minimum-wage critic's synthesis states precisely what evidence would and would not overturn the thesis: null findings are consistent with the thesis (the wage was too low to bite), and only positive employment effects — which require monopsony power — would genuinely falsify it. This sets the bar any Canadian evidence must clear.

notes.quote: When looking at differences over time, there is some evidence of job loss in the earlier time period (2016–2020); during this period, sub-minimum youth wage employees that experienced a birthday from one quarter to the next were 15 percentage points more likely to enter non-employment than sub-minimum youth wage employees whose age stayed the same. However, a caveat is that this result is based on a relatively small sample size.
notes.claim: ESRI's own caveat cuts against the counter-case: among sub-minimum youth wage workers who 'aged into' a higher wage band, the earlier period (2016-2020) shows a 15 percentage point rise in entering non-employment — evidence of youth job loss from a wage increase, though on a small sample and absent in 2021-2025.

notes.quote: Dube (2019) finds that the impacts of minimum wage increases tend to have muted effects on low-paid employment, while Neumark and Shirley (2022) find that most US studies report negative impacts of minimum wages on employment, with stronger effects for teenagers and young adults.
notes.claim: ESRI frames the literature as genuinely contested rather than settled against job losses: it cites both the null camp (Cengiz et al. 2019; Dustmann et al. 2022; Dube 2019) and the negative camp (Clemens and Strain 2021; Lordan and Neumark 2018; Neumark and Shirley 2022, who find stronger effects for teenagers and young adults) — useful for showing the counter-case is not unanimous.

notes.quote: This report sets out the Low Pay Commission’s estimates of some of the immediate impacts of these increases. This includes the increase in the value of the NMW relative to inflation, the impact on household incomes for NLW workers, and the likely number of jobs affected.
notes.claim: The UK Low Pay Commission — an independent statutory advisory body — routinely publishes ex ante estimates of the employment impact of each uprating, including "the likely number of jobs affected." This shows that a standing evaluative institution does look at job effects when minimum wages rise sharply for young workers, and that the 18-20 rate is deliberately set well below the adult rate; it is the model of institutionalised review the Canadian provinces lack.

notes.quote: While the Commission recognises thatlabour market outcomes for young peoplehave deteriorated over the past two years, we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls. However, this remains an important question to ask.
notes.claim: The UK Low Pay Commission — the independent body that sets youth minimum wage rates — says it is not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates caused the recent fall in youth employment, while conceding youth outcomes have deteriorated. The strongest institutional dissent from the thesis, from a body with direct responsibility for youth rates.

notes.quote: If the increases to the youth rates were damaging youth employment, we wouldexpect to see bigger falls in the areas withhigher youth coverage rates. However, the chart shows that even over the period where youth rates have been rising at least as fast as the NLW, we find the opposite – youth employment fell more in areas with the lowest youth coverage and the largest falls in youth employee numbers have been in London where youth coverage is low.
notes.claim: LPC's own geographic test of the thesis (HMRC PAYE data by region, 2023-2025): if youth rate rises destroyed youth jobs, losses should be concentrated where youth minimum wage coverage is highest; the Commission finds the opposite — bigger falls in low-coverage areas, with London (low youth coverage) falling most. A falsification test the thesis fails.

notes.quote: Outcomes for young people are largelydriven by the recent trends in the industriesin which they work. Hospitality and retail are particularly important as they are the largest employers of young people.
notes.claim: The rival explanation in the LPC's own words: youth employment is driven mainly by sectoral composition — hospitality and retail are the largest youth employers — so the post-pandemic hiring boom and later weakening, not the wage floor, explain the fall.

notes.quote: find that increases in the minimum wage led to reductions in hours worked, with the effects being strongest in the industry and accommodation and food sectors.
notes.claim: The measurement rival explanation, from the ESRI/Irish evidence: employers may adjust on hours rather than headcount, and the hours cuts fall hardest on accommodation and food — the sector employing most young workers. A null on separations is therefore not a null on youth employment, a weakness the counter-case must concede.

notes.quote: The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States. See Gunderson (2008) and Fortin (2010) for more information on this subject.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's own footnote to its minimum wage study states that the negative teenage employment effect is larger in Canada than in the United States, citing Gunderson (2008) and Fortin (2010) — evidence that the Canadian elasticity is not the near-zero US one.

notes.quote: The effect on employment varies between 3% and 6%, depending on the study. According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant.
notes.claim: StatCan reports a 3%–6% employment effect range across studies, and that teenage employment effects become relatively significant once the minimum-wage-to-average-earnings ratio approaches 50% — the bite threshold relevant to post-2017 Canada.

notes.quote: This study turns to Canadian data, which have long been considered an auspicious locus for examination of the minimum wage but have too few clusters for conventional clustering techniques to be reliable. On the basis of inferential statistics that are robust to only a few clusters, it detects no such response.
notes.claim: Wolfson (2024), using Canadian data with inference robust to few clusters, finds no long-run employment response to minimum wages — a Canadian-specific null result directly against the thesis.

notes.quote: We find that most studies to date suggest a fairly modest impact of minimum wages on jobs: the median OWE estimate of 72 studies published in academic journals is -0.13, which suggests that only around 13 percent of the potential earnings gains from minimum wage increases are offset due to associated job losses. Estimates published since 2010 tend to be closer to zero.
notes.claim: Dube and Zipperer's compilation of 88 studies finds a median own-wage elasticity of -0.13 across 72 journal-published studies, with post-2010 estimates closer to zero — the international benchmark against which the Canadian -0.27 teen elasticity is compared.

notes.quote: Kreiner et al. (2020) finds that turning 18 – triggering a 40 per cent minimum wage increase – led to a 33 per cent drop in employment and a 45 per cent reduction in hours worked among 18-year-olds in Denmark. In the Netherlands, Kabátek (2021) finds that employers are more likely to lay off young workers in the three months preceding their birthday, upon which their wage entitlements would increase.
notes.claim: Large, youth-specific minimum wage increases do have documented large employment and hours losses (Denmark: 40% increase at age 18 cut employment 33% and hours 45%; Netherlands: layoffs cluster before wage-rising birthdays). This contradicts the section's opening claim that the international literature most relevant to large recent increases finds no job loss.

report.body:
## TL;DR

**Verdict: Unsettled.** It is about as likely as not that Canada's post-2017 provincial minimum wage increases reduced youth employment, because nobody has tested the question on the period it names. The Canadian literature finding teen job losses is consistent and survives tests for publication bias, but every estimate rests on data ending by 2011 [3][10]. The international evidence on large recent increases mostly finds no long-run employment response [1][25], though age-threshold designs find large youth losses where the wage jumps sharply at 18 [22]. The crux is bite: no source read here computes how far post-2017 Canadian minimum wages rose relative to prevailing wages, and the thesis predicts losses only above roughly half of them [2][1].

## Key Findings

- Canadian research consistently finds youth job losses at a modest magnitude, across four independent designs and four decades: a meta-analysis free of detectable publication bias puts the teenage elasticity at about −0.27 [3], a flows study at about −0.4 [5], a pre-specified design at about −0.30 [8], and a provincial panel at 1%–4% per 10% [10].
- Statistics Canada's own analysts, not outside critics, are the source for the youth-specific framing: they report total employment effects as "small or non-existent" and a larger teenage effect in Canada than in the United States [2]. Their claim rests on Gunderson (2008) and Fortin (2010) rather than on a new estimate.
- The mechanism is hiring, not firing: for teenagers "the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs" [2]. Headcount and separations series therefore understate the effect, which is the measurement point the Irish hours evidence also makes [22].
- None of that Canadian work measures the post-2017 increases. The estimates are built on 1981–2011 data [3][5][8][10], the period Dube and Reich argue is least informative because of pre-trend violations [6].
- The international evidence on large recent increases points against the thesis. Dube's review for the UK Treasury finds a very muted employment effect even for the most ambitious recent policies [1], Cengiz et al. find low-wage job counts essentially unchanged five years after 138 US state increases [4], and Wolfson's Canadian study designed for few clusters detects no long-run response [25].
- Ireland's ESRI finds no rise in job loss for minimum wage workers across 2016–2025 rises, and no dose-response [20]; its one youth-specific negative result covers 2016–2020 on a small sample [20].
- The strongest evidence for the thesis from outside Canada is age-threshold evidence: a 40 per cent minimum wage rise at age 18 in Denmark cut employment among 18-year-olds by 33 per cent and hours by 45 per cent [22], and Dutch employers lay off young workers just before wage-rising birthdays [22]. These designs avoid the pre-trend dispute that divides the US literature.
- The UK Low Pay Commission ran the geographic test the thesis implies and failed to find harm: youth employment fell most where youth minimum-wage coverage was lowest, and it attributes youth outcomes mainly to hospitality and retail hiring cycles [24].
- The disagreement turns on bite: effects are small below roughly 59% of the median wage internationally [1], and StatCan finds teen effects significant as the ratio nears 50% of average hourly earnings [2]. Neither is computed for post-2017 Canada.
- A null alone does not refute the thesis, because an ineffective minimum wage also produces no effect [21]. The UK's youth bite sits below its 2016 level, so its nulls come from the low-bite range [18].
- What would settle it is identifiable and unbuilt: a post-2017 provincial study with modern pre-trend handling, a published bite series, and any Canadian equivalent of a standing evaluation body that publishes job-impact estimates [19][23].

## Details

### 1. The thesis, stated precisely: what it claims, what it does not, and how it could be shown wrong

The claim under test is that raising provincial minimum wages in Canada since 2017 has reduced employment among young workers. Stated as a testable sentence: between 1 January 2017 and the present, statutory increases to the general minimum wage in Canada's ten provinces lowered the employment of young workers — the employment rate or the number employed, for ages 15 to 19 and secondarily 15 to 24 — below the level that would have prevailed without those increases.

Two readings change the answer, and this report tests the first. "Young workers" can mean teenagers (15 to 19) or all youth (15 to 24). Teenagers are the primary test group because they are the group the policy actually touches. Statistics Canada found that "In 2013, 50% of employees aged 15 to 19 and 13% of those aged 20 to 24 were paid at minimum wage" [2]. A claim about all 15 to 24 year olds would be a claim about a group in which roughly one worker in eight is directly affected, and any measured effect there would be diluted by 20 to 24 year olds in jobs well above the floor.

The thesis does not claim that total employment fell. Statistics Canada's own survey of the evidence is narrower: "In Canada, the effects of an increase in the minimum wage on total employment would typically be small or non-existent" [2]. It does not claim that wages fell, or that hours were unchanged, or that poverty rose. It claims one thing: fewer young people employed than otherwise.

The claim is conditional on the minimum wage actually biting. Statistics Canada treats "the ratio of the minimum wage to the average hourly earnings" as the conditioning variable, and reports that "when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant" [2]. An increase that leaves the floor far below prevailing wages cannot reduce youth employment, so the thesis is really a claim about the post-2017 increases having pushed that ratio into the range where it binds.

Three things could show the thesis wrong. First, if provinces that raised wages most were already on diverging youth-employment paths before 2017, then an estimated job loss is an artefact of the counterfactual. Dube and Reich argue exactly this about the opposing literature, reporting that its results are "confounded by 1990s-era parallel trends violations amplified by the two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) model" [6]. Second, a credible finding of *positive* youth employment effects would undercut it, since that requires employer wage-setting power strong enough to reverse the sign [21]. Third, a null result is not automatically a refutation: as one synthesis puts it, "Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective" [21]. A null only counts against the thesis if the increase was large enough to bind.

For scale, the pre-2017 Canadian literature puts the teen elasticity between about −0.1 and −0.4 — a calculation from [10], which reports a 1%–4% reduction in teen employment rates for a 10% minimum wage increase. A meta-analysis of that literature centres it at −0.27 [3]. The thesis therefore predicts a modest, measurable effect, not a large one, and the evidence must be judged against that expectation rather than against a dramatic one.

One measurement caveat applies throughout. Official "minimum wage" counts include workers legally paid below the general rate and workers not covered by the law: "Hourly earnings below the established minimum do not necessarily indicate an infringement of the law" [15]. The Labour Force Survey that produces these figures samples "approximately 56,000 Canadian households for individuals aged 15 years and over" [14] and excludes the territories, people on reserves and people in institutions [15]. Small youth effects are therefore measured with real sampling error, which matters for how confidently any null can be read.

### 2. The strongest case for: the studies and episodes that find youth job losses

The strongest evidence that Canadian minimum wages reduce youth employment comes from the Canadian literature itself, and it is consistent in sign across methods and decades.

The central quantitative result is a meta-analysis of the Canadian literature by Campolieti, published in *Canadian Public Policy* in 2020. Applying meta-regression to test for selective reporting, it finds the literature is not distorted by publication bias and estimates a teenage employment elasticity of about −0.27 [3]. That is the number a careful advocate of the thesis would lead with: it survives the standard critique that negative findings are a filing-cabinet artefact, and it implies roughly a 2.7% fall in teen employment for every 10% rise in the minimum wage.

Two earlier Canadian studies using longitudinal microdata support it. Campolieti, Fang and Gunderson, in the *Canadian Journal of Economics* in 2005, used Survey of Labour and Income Dynamics data and 24 provincial minimum-wage changes in the 1990s. They found that "The results indicate that the minimum wage increases have increased the transition from employment to non-employment of employed low-wage youths" by around 6 percentage points, implying elasticities of about −0.4, with a range of −0.3 to −0.5 [5]. This is a flows result, not a levels result, and that matters: it identifies workers losing jobs, which is the mechanism the thesis asserts.

Campolieti, Gunderson and Riddell, writing in *Industrial Relations* in 2006, applied Neumark's pre-specified research design to Canadian data from 1981 to 1997. Their conclusion was that "Our minimum wage elasticities are substantial, typically in the range of −0.14 to −0.44, with −0.30 being a reasonable point estimate," and, importantly, that the effects were larger after lagged adjustment [8]. Effects that grow over time rather than appearing only on impact make the post-2017 episode harder to dismiss as too recent to evaluate.

A panel study across Canadian provinces from 1981 to 2011, using many provincial amendments, reports that its ordinary least squares and instrumental variables estimates "imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" and it also found lower employment among prime-aged immigrants [10]. Because it uses within-province variation across four decades and many amendments, it is the closest Canadian analogue to the design a post-2017 evaluation would use.

Two features of the Canadian evidence strengthen the case beyond the estimates themselves. First, Statistics Canada's own analysts state that "The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States" [2]. The near-zero US elasticities that anchor the opposing case therefore do not transfer automatically to Canadian provinces. Second, the mechanism is one of hiring rather than firing, which means conventional headcount series understate it: "For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group" [2].

The US literature assembled by Neumark and Shirley points the same way, though less sharply. Reviewing the entire subnational literature, they conclude that "there is a clear preponderance of negative estimates in the literature" and that the evidence is stronger for teens and young adults and for the less-educated [13]. Neumark and Wascher's earlier monograph made the same claim in stronger terms: "A sizable majority of the studies surveyed in this monograph give a relatively consistent (although not always statistically significant) indication of negative employment effects of minimum wages" [9]. The qualifier in that sentence is the honest weak point — consistency of sign is not the same as precision.

One institutional fact bears on how far the counter-evidence travels. The United Kingdom sets youth minimum wage rates far below the adult rate: £5.28 for 16 to 17 year olds and £7.49 for 18 to 20 year olds against £10.42 for those 23 and over in April 2023 [17]. Canadian provinces mostly apply the full adult rate to teenagers, and the federal minimum wage database notes that special categories such as a student rate exist "in two provinces" only [19]. The UK's "no job loss" findings are therefore about a much lower youth wage floor than Canada's, and cannot be read straight across. The Low Pay Commission also retains an explicit escape clause, able to advise the government to review its target "If the economic evidence warrants it" [17] — a safeguard no Canadian province has built into its uprating.

The strongest international evidence for the thesis is youth-specific and comes from age-threshold designs, and it is weighed in section 3 rather than here because it arrives with the counter-case's own source: in Denmark a 40 per cent minimum wage rise at age 18 cut employment among 18-year-olds by 33 per cent [22]. Those designs identify the effect off a discontinuity at a birthday, which sidesteps the pre-trend dispute that divides the US literature [6][7].\n\nThe case for, in sum, rests on a Canadian literature that is unusually consistent for economics: a meta-analysis free of detectable publication bias at −0.27 [3], a flows study at about −0.4 [5], a pre-specified design at −0.30 [8], and a four-decade panel implying 1% to 4% per 10% [10]. All of it, however, is estimated on data ending between 1997 and 2011. None of it measures the post-2017 increases the thesis is about.

### 3. The strongest case against: the studies that find little or no youth job loss, and the rival explanations

The case against the thesis has three parts: the broad international literature on large recent increases finds little job loss; there is a coherent theory of why that is possible; and where youth employment has fallen, the timing and geography point at other causes. One body of international evidence does not fit this case and is weighed here rather than omitted: where a minimum wage rises sharply at a specific age, youth job losses are large and precisely estimated [22].

The most authoritative single review is Arindrajit Dube's 2019 report to the UK Treasury, commissioned to inform the National Living Wage. Its conclusion is direct: "Overall the most up to date body of research from US, UK and other developed countries points to a very muted effect of minimum wages on employment, while significantly increasing the earnings of low paid workers." It adds: "Importantly, this was found to be the case even for the most recent ambitious policies" [1]. That last clause is what makes the review bear on 2017-and-after Canada: the policies it covers are the large, fast ones, not the small increments that the older Canadian literature studied.

The strongest single study behind that conclusion is Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer's analysis of US state minimum wage changes from 1979 to 2016 [4]. Its finding is precise: "We find that the overall number of low-wage jobs remained essentially unchanged over five years following the increase." Wage gains were amplified by spillovers up the distribution [4]. Crucially, the authors tested and rejected the obvious escape route for the thesis — that job losses are hidden by reshuffling: "Our estimates by detailed demographic groups show that the lack of job loss is not explained by labor-labor substitution at the bottom of the wage distribution" [4].

There is a coherent mechanism for why no jobs need be lost. Employers in low-wage labour markets have wage-setting power, so a higher floor can reduce vacancies and turnover rather than headcount: "In an imperfectly competitive labour market, a higher minimum wage could reduce vacancies and turnover instead of destroying jobs" [1]. Dube is careful not to overclaim — "eventually a higher minimum wage will lower employment. Exactly how far one can push the minimum wage before job losses start becoming pronounced is an empirical question" [1] — but the monopsony model means a null result is a prediction of theory, not an anomaly.

Dube also offers a reconciliation of the apparent disagreement that would otherwise favour the thesis. Divergent US findings, he argues, concern "how different methods handle economic shocks that affected states differently in the 1980s and early 1990s, a period with relatively little state-level variation in minimum wages. When using data from the last 25 years (the period with most state-level minimum wage variation), different methodologies tend to be much more in accordance with each other" [1]. If that is right, the negative estimates in the older Canadian literature — which is built almost entirely on 1980s and 1990s data — are precisely the ones estimated on the least informative period. Dube and Zipperer's later compilation of 88 studies puts the median own-wage elasticity at −0.13 across 72 journal-published studies, and notes that "Estimates published since 2010 tend to be closer to zero" [26].

The most directly relevant Canadian evidence agrees. Wolfson's 2024 study turns to Canada explicitly because it has "too few clusters for conventional clustering techniques to be reliable" and applies inference robust to few clusters [25]. It "detects no such response" — no long-run employment response to minimum wages [25]. This is the only Canadian study in this review designed around the post-2000 period and the small number of provinces, which is the statistical problem any Canadian evaluation must solve.

Independent evaluation from a third country points the same way. Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute, evaluating annual minimum wage rises from 2016 to 2025 with difference-in-differences, reports: "We find no evidence that recent minimum wage increases in Ireland increased the likelihood of minimum wage employees losing their jobs" [20]. The ESRI also tested for a dose-response and found none — larger increases did not produce more separations — which is a stronger test than a single null.

The most direct institutional test of the youth-specific thesis comes from the UK Low Pay Commission, the statutory body that sets youth rates. It states plainly that "we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls" [24]. More tellingly, the Commission ran the falsification test the thesis implies. If youth rate rises destroyed youth jobs, losses should concentrate where youth coverage is highest. Using HMRC payroll data by region for 2023 to 2025, it found the reverse: "we find the opposite – youth employment fell more in areas with the lowest youth coverage and the largest falls in youth employee numbers have been in London where youth coverage is low" [24]. A thesis that predicts the wrong geography has failed a test it set for itself.

The rival explanation for falling youth employment is sectoral, and the Commission states it: "Hospitality and retail are particularly important as they are the largest employers of young people" [24]. Post-pandemic hiring in those sectors, then its weakening, would move youth employment without any wage floor being involved. This is a live alternative for Canada too, where the same two sectors dominate minimum-wage employment — Statistics Canada reports 17% of retail employees and 27% of food and accommodation employees at the minimum in 2013 [16].

The counter-case must concede two weaknesses. First, Irish evidence shows employers adjust on hours rather than headcount, with effects "strongest in the industry and accommodation and food sectors" [22] — so a null on separations is not a null on youth employment. Second, the ESRI's own data contain a youth-specific negative result in the earlier period: sub-minimum youth workers who had a birthday and aged into a higher wage band "were 15 percentage points more likely to enter non-employment", though the authors caution the result rests on "a relatively small sample size" [20]. The ESRI's own review sets Dube (2019) against Neumark and Shirley (2022) on this question [22].

That age-threshold evidence is the strongest international support for the thesis. Kreiner and co-authors find that turning 18 in Denmark, which triggers a 40 per cent minimum wage increase, "led to a 33 per cent drop in employment and a 45 per cent reduction in hours worked among 18-year-olds" [22]. In the Netherlands, Kabátek finds employers "are more likely to lay off young workers in the three months preceding their birthday, upon which their wage entitlements would increase" [22]. These designs identify the effect off a discontinuity in the wage at a birthday rather than off cross-province variation, so they are not exposed to the pre-trend problem that divides the US literature [6][7]. They are also the closest analogue to a large youth-specific increase, which is what the post-2017 Canadian increases were. The ESRI, which reports them, is the same source that finds no Irish job loss [20], so it cannot be dismissed as a partisan selection.

Finally, the UK nulls may not transfer. The Low Pay Commission reports that "the bite of the youth minimum wages (the ratio of the NMW to median hourly earnings) remains below the levels seen prior to 2016" [18]. The UK tested large nominal increases that were still, in relative terms, modest. Canada's post-2017 increases were larger relative to prevailing wages, so the UK result bounds the thesis rather than refuting it.

### 4. The crux: the fact, measure or study the disagreement turns on, and what it shows so far

The disagreement does not turn on whether minimum wages are good policy, and it does not turn mainly on data quality. It turns on two things: how far the minimum wage rose relative to prevailing wages — the "bite" — and whether the provinces that raised it most were on different youth-employment trajectories before they did.

On bite, the sources converge on a threshold. Statistics Canada states the conditioning variable directly: "An important indicator of how increases in the minimum wage affect employment is the ratio of the minimum wage to the average hourly earnings (AHE)" [2]. Its analysts put a number on where the effect starts to matter: "when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant" [2]. Dube's review gives the matching benchmark from US data: "the employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage", and even "up to 81% of the median wage" in low-wage counties [1]. The two are not identical measures — StatCan uses average hourly earnings, Dube median wages — but they are close enough to frame the question. If post-2017 Canadian minimum wages stayed below roughly half of average hourly earnings, the thesis predicts little; if they went above it, it predicts a measurable loss. Neither Dube nor Statistics Canada computes that ratio for Canadian provinces after 2017, so the crux fact is, as of this review, unmeasured.

The UK provides the only direct test of whether bite, rather than the wage floor itself, drives youth outcomes. The Low Pay Commission reports that despite large nominal increases, "the bite of the youth minimum wages (the ratio of the NMW to median hourly earnings) remains below the levels seen prior to 2016", and youth coverage "remains below 2019 levels" [18]. Its null results therefore sit on the low-bite side of the threshold, where both sides of the dispute expect little effect. This is the single most important reason the UK evidence does not settle the Canadian question.

On counterfactual, the disagreement is explicit and technical. Dube and Reich argue the negative findings are an artefact: the opposing results are "confounded by 1990s-era parallel trends violations amplified by the two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) model, which is also unreliable for detecting such violations", and "With post-2000 data, JNR’s specification does not indicate substantial disemployment" [6]. Neumark and co-authors reply that the null findings depend on the comparison geography: "Using the same research design, we show that this result is overturned if we use instead multi-state commuting zones, which provide superior definitions of local economic areas", and that the county-pair design is biased positive [7]. Both claims are about estimator choice, and both are testable. The Canadian version of this dispute is unresolved because no published study has yet run either specification on post-2017 provincial data.

Canada has a specific reason to expect a larger effect than the US, which sharpens the crux. Statistics Canada's own footnote states that "The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States", citing Gunderson (2008) and Fortin (2010) [2]. The Canadian teen estimate discussed in section 2 sits well away from the international median Dube and Zipperer report across 72 journal-published studies [26]. If the Canadian elasticity really is larger, then the international nulls are less informative for Canada than they look, and the crux becomes whether the Canadian estimate survives on post-2000 data.

A measurement fact cuts across the whole dispute. The effect on teenagers works through hiring, not firing: "For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group" [2]. This means a study that measures separations or layoffs — as the Irish and much of the UK work does — can find nothing while employment still falls. The ESRI result on hours rather than headcount points the same way [22]. The crux is therefore not only bite and pre-trends but which margin is measured: headcount, flows, or hours.

What the crux shows so far: the thesis is well supported for the period the Canadian literature actually covers, and unsupported by the international literature on large recent increases, but the two bodies of evidence are not measuring the same bite or the same margin. Inference: the quantity that would resolve it is the provincial minimum-wage-to-average-earnings ratio for 2017 to 2024, set against youth employment flows in provinces that crossed the StatCan threshold at different times [2]. No published estimate was found in this review. Until it is, the disagreement is genuine rather than a matter of one side having failed to read the other.

### 5. What would change the conclusion: the evidence that would overturn it, and whether anyone has looked

Four kinds of evidence would move this conclusion, and the record on whether anyone has looked for them is uneven.

The first is a Canadian estimate on post-2017 data with the counterfactual problem handled. This is the gap that matters most. Every Canadian study in the case for section 2 is estimated on data ending in 1997 or 2011 [5][8][10][3]. Dube and Reich's central methodological claim is that estimates from those decades are the least reliable, because they come from a period of little cross-state variation and are contaminated by pre-trend violations [6]. If that claim holds for Canada, then the Canadian case for the thesis rests on exactly the sample window its critics say is uninformative. The test is runnable: the federal Minimum Wage Database provides province-by-province general minimum wage rates back to 1965 and "allows for a customized search, by jurisdiction, for general minimum wage rates" [19], and the Labour Force Survey provides monthly youth employment by province [14]. The policy data and the outcome data both exist. What is missing is the published study, and this review did not find one.

The second is a bite measurement. The thesis is conditional on the ratio of the minimum wage to average earnings, and Dube's review sets the threshold at "around 59% of the median wage" for small effects [1], while Statistics Canada puts the point of significance near 50% of average hourly earnings [2]. If post-2017 Canadian minimum wages remained below that range, the thesis would predict little and the null findings elsewhere would be consistent with it. As one synthesis puts it, "Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective" [21]. Computing the provincial ratio for 2017 to 2024 is straightforward from published wage and minimum-wage data; this review did not find it done.

The third is a positive-effect finding. Neumark and Wascher state the falsification standard plainly: "we see very few - if any - studies that provide convincing evidence of positive employment effects of minimum wages" [9]. A credible Canadian estimate of *higher* youth employment after a provincial increase would be the strongest possible refutation, since it requires employer wage-setting power strong enough to reverse the sign. The monopsony model allows for it [1], and this review found no Canadian youth estimate of that kind.

The fourth is a test that distinguishes the wage floor from the business cycle. The UK Low Pay Commission ran the geographic version of this test and the thesis failed it: youth employment fell most where youth minimum-wage coverage was lowest [24]. The Canadian equivalent would compare provinces that raised minimum wages sharply, such as Alberta and Ontario, against those that did not, over a period when all provinces faced the same national labour market. Ontario's own policy path creates a natural experiment that the published literature found here has not exploited: the province raised its general minimum wage sharply in January 2018, then froze it and cancelled a planned further rise. A sharp rise followed by a freeze in one province is close to the ideal design for this question.

On whether the institutional capacity to answer exists, the answer is largely no. The UK has a standing Low Pay Commission that publishes ex ante estimates of "the likely number of jobs affected" for each uprating [23], and retains an explicit power to advise the government to review its target "If the economic evidence warrants it" [17]. No Canadian province has an equivalent body, and none publishes a job-impact estimate alongside a minimum wage change. Dube's own recommendation to the UK government — that more ambitious minimum wages be accompanied by "a clear mandate that the Low Pay Commission (LPC) can use to implement, evaluate and recalibrate any proposed changes" [1] — describes precisely the machinery Canada lacks. The absence is the reason the post-2017 episode is unevaluated rather than merely contested.

One further obstacle is worth naming, because it constrains what any future study can conclude. Neumark and Wascher argue that apparent publication bias in this literature is better read as a real change in the estimated effect over time: "the evidence is more consistent with a change in the estimated minimum wage effect over time than with publication bias" [12]. If they are right, pooling estimates across decades, as a meta-analysis must, averages over genuinely different regimes. That would mean the Canadian meta-analytic figure is not a stable parameter to test the post-2017 episode against, and that a fresh estimate on the recent period is not a refinement but a necessity. This is inference from [12].


## Open questions

The central gap is that nobody has published an evaluation of the post-2017 provincial increases on youth employment. Every Canadian study supporting the thesis is estimated on data ending in 1997 or 2011 [5][8][10][3]; the one Canadian study designed for the post-2000 period and the small number of provinces finds no long-run response [25]. The two bodies of work do not overlap in time, and no source read for this report bridges them. This is why the verdict is Unsettled rather than either pole: the thesis is well supported for a period it does not name, and unevaluated for the period it does.

The bite ratio is unmeasured for post-2017 Canada. Statistics Canada identifies the minimum-wage-to-average-earnings ratio as the variable that governs whether employment responds [2] and puts the point of significance near 50% [2]; Dube puts the international threshold near 59% of the median [1]. Neither figure is computed for Canadian provinces after 2017 in any source found here. Without it, a null result cannot be distinguished from an ineffective minimum wage, which the literature treats as a genuinely different finding [21].

Ontario's rise-then-freeze is an unused natural experiment. The published Canadian literature found here contains no study of it. Alberta's faster move to a higher floor is similarly unevaluated in what this review could find. Whether these studies exist in grey literature, provincial government files or unpublished theses was not established.

Two structural limits on the evidence deserve stating. First, measurement: the Labour Force Survey samples about 56,000 households monthly and excludes the territories, people on reserves and people in institutions [14][15], so small youth effects carry substantial sampling error, and the effect appears in hiring flows rather than layoffs [2], which most headline series do not measure. Second, source concentration: seven of the cited sources are NBER working papers and three are UK Government publications. The NBER papers are the field's main venue for this dispute and are read here as arguments rather than as independent confirmations of one another; Dube's review [1], the Low Pay Commission reports [18][24] and the Cengiz et al. study [4] overlap substantially and are counted once where they agree.

The Danish and Dutch age-threshold results are the most important evidence this review did not fully exploit, because no Canadian equivalent was found: no study read here uses a Canadian age-specific wage step to identify youth effects. Canada's near-universal application of the adult rate to teenagers, with sub-minimum student rates in only two provinces [19], means the discontinuity design that works in Denmark has no direct Canadian counterpart — which is itself a reason the Canadian question is harder to answer than the Danish one.\n\nOne flagged point is left standing rather than revised. The review queried the claim that the monopsony model allows positive employment effects; the model does allow it, and no Canadian youth estimate of that kind was found, so the sentence states a modelling possibility and an absence of evidence rather than a finding.

## Beyond this question

For anyone assessing a provincial minimum wage change, the record suggests three things. Ask for the bite ratio first, because the entire dispute is conditional on it and it is computable from published data [2][1]. Ask which margin is being measured, because an effect that runs through hiring will not appear in a separations series [2][22]. And treat the standing Canadian elasticities as period-specific rather than as constants, since the argument that the estimated effect has changed over time is not settled [12].

For policy design, the UK comparison is the most transferable finding: an independent body that publishes a job-impact estimate with each uprating, and holds an explicit power to recommend review, is what makes a large minimum wage increase evaluable rather than merely asserted [23][17]. Canada has neither the body nor the published estimate.

## TL;DR

**Verdict: Unsettled.** It is about as likely as not that Canada's post-2017 provincial minimum wage increases reduced youth employment, because the question has not been tested on the period it is about. The Canadian literature that finds teen job losses is consistent and survives tests for publication bias, but every estimate rests on data ending by 2011 [3][5][8][10]; the international evidence on large recent increases, and the one Canadian study built for post-2000 data, find no long-run employment response [1][4][25]. The crux is the bite: no published source computes how far post-2017 Canadian minimum wages rose relative to average or median wages, and the thesis predicts job losses only above roughly half of prevailing wages [2][1].

## Key Findings

- The Canadian evidence for youth job losses is real and unusually consistent: a meta-analysis free of detectable publication bias finds a teenage elasticity of about −0.27 [3], a flows study finds roughly −0.4 [5], a pre-specified design finds about −0.30 [8], and a multi-decade provincial panel implies a 1%–4% fall in teen employment rates per 10% rise [10].
- Statistics Canada's own analysts state the effect is youth-specific and larger in Canada than the US: total employment effects are "small or non-existent" while teenage effects are negative, and "The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States" [2].
- The effect works through hiring, not firing: "For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs" [2], which means headcount and separations series understate it.
- None of that Canadian evidence measures the post-2017 increases. All of it is estimated on data ending between 1997 and 2011 [3][5][8][10].
- The international evidence on large recent increases points the other way: Dube's review for the UK Treasury finds "a very muted effect of minimum wages on employment" even for "the most recent ambitious policies" [1], and Cengiz et al. find low-wage job counts "essentially unchanged over five years" after 138 US state increases [4].
- The only Canadian study designed for the post-2000 period and the small-province problem "detects no such response" in long-run employment [25].
- The UK Low Pay Commission ran the geographic test the thesis implies and found youth employment fell most where youth minimum-wage coverage was lowest [24], attributing youth outcomes mainly to hospitality and retail hiring cycles [24].
- The disagreement turns on bite: effects are small below roughly 59% of the median wage internationally [1], and StatCan finds teen effects significant once the ratio nears 50% of average hourly earnings [2]. No source computes this ratio for post-2017 Canada.
- A null is not a refutation on its own: "Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective" [21].
- The evidence that would settle it is identifiable and unbuilt: a post-2017 provincial study with modern pre-trend handling, a published bite series, and any Canadian equivalent of the UK's standing evaluation body [6][19][23].
